A PROCLAMATION
Honoring the Life and Legacy of Marco Perez-Vazquez
1 WHEREAS, In Fall 2025, Florida State University lost a beloved and extraordinary member of our
2 campus community, Marco Perez-Vazquez; and
3 WHEREAS, Marco dedicated his time here at Florida State University to serving and uplifting every
4 student he shared space with, forging lasting bonds with the Florida State University student body,
5 one student at a time; and
6 WHEREAS, Marco's passion for the Florida State University student body led him to act in various
7 leadership roles. Marco welcomed first-year students with energy as a 2023 Orientation Leader,
8 later stepping into a similar role as a CARE Summer Bridge 2024 Ambassador. He was desk
9 support staff for University Housing from 2023-2024. In 2023, Marco became a brother of the Beta
10 Iota Chapter of Lambda Theta Phi Latin Fraternity, Inc., thereafter, acting as Chapter President
11 from 2024-2025. He led the Cuban American Student Association and Puerto-Rican Student
12 Association as an involved member on their executive boards and was Programming Coordinator
13 for the Hispanic/Latine Student Union. Marco was honored as a Garnet and Gold Key Member,
14 Florida State University's oldest and most prestigious leadership society. As of late, Marco was an
15 Investigative Intern at the Law Offices of the Public Defender, Jessica J. Yeary and worked as a
16 Southgate Assistant Resident Director. Within them all, Marco poured care; and
17 WHEREAS, Marco aspired to leave a mark on others through his work, and through conversation; and
18 WHEREAS, Marco was a great believer in others, showing them a path forward whenever needed; and
19 WHEREAS, Marco's influence had a lasting impact on these individuals, who are gathered herein to
20 give voice and memory to the lively character and contagious spirit of Marco Perez-Vazquez; and
21 WHEREAS, George Tsoucalas says, "I can confidently say that everybody who’s met Marco can name
22 something they admire about him. I can do so for hours. One of my most favorite things is Marco’s
23 ability to compliment people. He was able to find beauty in anyone. You’d be randomly talking and
24 he’d cut you off and say something like “That’s what I love about you ____, you’re so ___.” IDocusign Envelope ID: B090E3D0-3F9D-4E2A-9973-29EF76C8F359

This proclamation recognizes advisor Tanner McKinley on his receival of the New Employee of the

congratulate him on this recognition.

On April 9th, 2026, Tanner McKinley, Assistant Director of Policy & Budget Tanner McKinley received
the New Employee of the Year Award by the Division of Student Affairs. This proclamation honors that
recognition.

promise. Tanner's selection for this award is a reflection of the excellence he brings to his work31

Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation expresses the Florida State University Student Senate’s solidarity with the people of
Venezuela following the devastating earthquakes that struck the country on June 24, 2026. It
recognizes the humanitarian impact of the disaster, supports the relief efforts organized by the
Venezuelan Student Association and the Hispanic/Latine Student Union, and encourages Student
Senators and the broader FSU community to contribute to the donation drive and help raise awareness
across campus.
Background Information:
On June 24, 2026, Venezuela experienced two powerful earthquakes measuring magnitudes 7.2 and
7.5, occurring just seconds apart near Morón along the country’s Caribbean coast. The earthquakes
caused widespread destruction across northern Venezuela, including Caracas, La Guaira, Carabobo,
and surrounding coastal communities, making them among the strongest earthquakes to affect the
nation in more than a century.
As rescue and recovery efforts continue, thousands of families have been impacted by the destruction
and remain in need of humanitarian assistance. In response, the Venezuelan Student Association and
the Hispanic/Latine Student Union at Florida State University have organized a campus-wide donation
drive to support relief efforts and provide aid to those affected.

6 and,
7
8 WHEREAS, September 11, 2001, claimed the lives of 2,977 innocent people, including 343 firefighters
9 and paramedics, 23 New York City Police Officers, 37 Port Authority Police Officers, 125 Pentagon
10 Staff, and 261 flight passengers, forever changing the United States, reminding future generations of
11 the cost of hatred and the strength of the human spirit; and,
12
13 WHEREAS, amidst unimaginable tragedy, countless individuals displayed extraordinary courage,
14 including Rick Rescorla, who safely evacuated more than 2,700 Morgan Stanley employees before
15 returning to help others and sacrificing his life; and,
16
17 WHEREAS, bravery included Moira Smith, an NYPD officer who repeatedly entered the World Trade
18 Center to lead the injured to safety before losing her own life; and,
19
20 WHEREAS, bravery included Welles Crowther, the "Man in the Red Bandanna," who saved as many
21 as 18 people by climbing up the South Tower stairwell to floors above where United Airlines Flight 175
22 struck, guiding and carrying individuals to the safety of the staircases; and,
23
24 WHEREAS, bravery included Benjamin Clark, a chef at Fiduciary Trust Company, who successfully
25 helped evacuate the entire 96th floor, and was last seen helping a handicapped individual during the
26 collapse of the South Tower; and,
27
28 WHEREAS, bravery included John Perry, an NYPD officer who, despite being hours from retirement
29 and off-duty, rushed into the North Tower to help evacuate people, last seen helping a woman escape
30 the North Tower when it collapsed; and,
31

32 WHEREAS, bravery included Danny Lewin, who attempted to halt the hijackers of American Airlines
33 Flight 11, and was stabbed to death onboard the plane; and,
34
35 WHEREAS, bravery included Leonard Hatton, a former marine and volunteer firefighter, who sprung to
36 action outside of working hours to join the New York City firefighters as they evacuated the North
37 Tower. He was last seen in the North Tower when the building collapsed; and,
38
39 WHEREAS, bravery included William Rodriguez, a maintenance worker, who led firefighters up the
40 North Tower with the emergency exit keys, helping hundreds of people escape the tower; and,
41
42 WHEREAS, bravery included Ronald Bucca, a New York Fire Marshall who was found passed away in
43 the debris of the South Tower. His protective coat was found wrapped around several other civilians;
44 and,
45
46 WHEREAS, bravery included Jason Thomas and Dave Karnes, marines who rushed into the World
47 Trade Center to save two police officers under 20 feet of debris; and,
48
49 WHEREAS, bravery included Kathy Mazza, a port authority police officer captain, who worked to
50 evacuate people from the North Tower lobby, including carrying a disabled woman down into the lobby
51 with her team. She made extra exits by shooting out the lobby’s windows with her service weapon, and
52 her body was found in the collapsed rubble with the woman she attempted to save; and,
53
54 WHEREAS, bravery included officers Thomas Jurgens, Mitchel Wallace, and William Thompson, who
55 all jumped in from unrelated posts to evacuate an individual who suffered a heart attack, and another
56 who suffered a head injury. After numerous entries into the World Trade Center, they were told it was
57 unsafe for them to go in again. Defying orders, they went in to save more people. They did not return;
58 and,
59
60 WHEREAS, bravery included the passengers and crew of Flight 93, who fought back against the
61 plane’s hijackers to seize back control of the plane, causing it to crash into an empty Pennsylvania field,
62 preventing the striking of either the White House or Capitol Hill; and,
63
64 WHEREAS, bravery included the coast guard and civilian captains who rescued half a million civilians
65 from the soot and debris of the collapsed World Trade Center, ferrying them to safer areas around New
66 York City; and,
67
68 WHEREAS, bravery included rescue dogs and their handlers, who worked for 14-hour shifts for periods
69 up to four weeks, searching for survivors, including the final survivor identified by rescue dog Trakr,
70 Genelle Guzman-McMillan, who had been trapped under debris for 27 hours; and,
71

WHEREAS, these stories represent the thousands of first responders, service members, and ordinary
citizens whose courage, sacrifice, and compassion continue to inspire our nation; and,
WHEREAS, Florida State University is committed to preserving the memory of those lost on September
11 and encouraging future generations to uphold the values of service, resilience, and unity;
NOW THEREFORE BE IT PROCLAIMED by the 78th Student Senate at Florida State University that
September 11 shall be recognized as a Day of Remembrance to honor the victims, survivors, first
responders, and all whose lives were forever changed by the attacks.
BE IT FURTHER PROCLAIMED that: the Student Senate encourages the Florida State University
community to observe September 11 through remembrance, education, and service, ensuring that the
sacrifices and acts of courage displayed that day are never forgotten.
DONE AND ADOPTED by the 78th Student Senate at Florida State University this 9th of
September, 2026.

78th STUDENT SENATE
Legislation Cover Sheet
Senate Proclamation #: 018
Primary Sponsor(s): Aihe
Co-sponsor(s): Holliday, Bigenho, Macalintal, Nturubika
Short Title: Honoring the 2026 Achievements of FSU’s Residential Hall Leaders.
Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation serves to memorialize and celebrate the awards, honors, and responsibilities given
to our student representatives that attended the National Association of Colleges and Universities’
(NACURH) 2026 conference. Specific details about the awards given are mentioned in the legislation.
Background Information:
The Inter-Residence Hall Council (IRHC) and National Residence Hall Honorary (NRHH) are student-
led organizations at Florida State University dedicated to serving, advocating, and uplifting students
within the University’s residential communities. Through programming, collaboration with university
administration, leadership development, philanthropy, and advocacy, these organizations serve
students living on campus with opportunities to enhance FSU’s residence hall communities while
connecting with student leaders across the region and nation.
On May 21 through May 24, 2026, the National Association of College and University Residence Halls
(NACURH) hosted its annual conference, bringing together student leaders from colleges and
universities across the country for educational programming, leadership development, collaboration,
and overall, competition. Florida State University was represented at the conference by student leaders
from IRHC and NRHH, who participated in educational sessions, presented a response to the
conference case study, and represented the University throughout the conference.
The Florida State University delegation demonstrated exceptional leadership and achievement
throughout the conference, receiving recognition at both the conference and regional levels and earning
several individual honors. These accomplishments reflect the commitment of the student leaders who
represented Florida State University and the significance of the University’s residential leadership
community.
This proclamation is being presented to the Student Senate to formally recognize these student leaders
for their achievements, leadership, service, and exemplary representation of Florida State University at
the regional and national levels.

and representation of the University at the 2026 NACURH Annual Conference. The intention of the
proclamation is to publicly acknowledge the contributions of these residence hall leaders on behalf of
the 78th Student Senate.

Short Title: Recognizing September as Suicide Prevention Month
Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation seeks to recognize September as Suicide Prevention Month and aims to increase
awareness of suicide prevention. It highlights the importance of encouraging students to engage in
conversations surrounding mental health, reduce stigma associated with seeking mental-health
support, and promotes awareness of resources available to students who may be experiencing suicidal
thoughts, supporting someone in crisis, or grieving the loss of someone to suicide. The legislation
further addresses the need to foster a supportive campus community in which students feel connected
and empowered to seek assistance when needed.
Background Information:
In 2003, the International Association for Suicide Prevention and the World Health Organization
recognized September 10th as Suicide Prevention Day. This day of recognition needed more
awareness, which led to the recognition of the entire month of September as National Suicide
Prevention Month in 2008.
Historically, there has existed a stigma around the conversation of mental health, discouraging those
who need to reach out from doing so. The Student Senate encourages students who are struggling to
utilize the campus resources and organizations outlined. At Florida State, these conversations have
been encouraged with multiple resources available to struggling students and campaigns going around
to help promote all the incredible work that our various departments are doing to combat this issue
head on. We need to continue this love and encouragement as we navigate the intense timeline of our
collegiate careers.

Counseling & Psychological Services, SGA Secretary of Health, Wellness & Safety, Center for Health
Advocacy and Wellness

Short Title: To Recognize the Civil Rights Legacy of Florida State University and the
Contributions of the Civil Rights Institute
Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation recognizes the 250th Anniversary of American Independence as an
opportunity to reflect on the nation's ongoing pursuit of civil rights while honoring Florida State
University's civil rights legacy and the contributions of the Civil Rights Institute. It asserts the
Student Senate's commitment to promoting civic engagement, historical education, equal
opportunity, and continued student participation in programs and initiatives that preserve and
advance civil rights for all members of the FSU community.
Background Information:
The United States celebrated its 250th Anniversary of Independence this year. As we
commemorate this historic landmark, it is important that we—as a Student Senate and Student
Body—reflect not only on the nation’s founding ideals but also on its continual pursuit of equal
justice, opportunity for all, and civil rights.
According to Merriam-Webster’s dictionary, civil rights are “rights that citizens are guaranteed
by their government through legislation or other actions to ensure equal opportunities and
protection under the law, regardless of their race, religion, or sex.” In the Constitution, these
are personal liberty rights guaranteed to U.S. citizens under the 13th, 14th, and 15th
Amendments. Additionally, through the Civil Rights Movement, it advanced the cause of
equality through the efforts of educators, community leaders, advocates, and most importantly,
students. The works of these groups transformed institutions across the nation, with the
Supreme Court’s ruling in Brown v. Board of Education in 1954 a culmination of efforts along
with the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Florida State University has its own unique civil rights history, beginning with the integration of
the university in 1962 and continuing through the advocacy of students, faculty, alumni, and
community leaders to expand access, representation, and educational opportunity. The Civil
Rights Institute was founded in 2018 by alumni Doby Flowers and Fred Flowers, who,Docusign Envelope ID: 33807B2C-41A8-8935-8266-091B4C9EEB56

sections.heading: Page 2
sections.text:
approximately 60 years ago, contributed to FSU’s racial integration history with Fred Flowers .
We also recognize Ted Ellis, the inaugural director of FSU’s Civil Rights Institute. Since 2023,
Director Ellis has helped expand the institute’s programming, community partnerships, and
commitment to preserving and promoting civil rights history. Ted Ellis dedicated three years to
developing the infrastructure and early reputation of the institute. Through its establishment,
the University further strengthened its commitment to preserving this history through research,
education, dialogue, and community engagement.
Conversations surrounding the future of the Civil Rights Institute as a university resource for
students have highlighted the importance of ensuring students remain aware of the Institute’s
mission. It serves to promote civil rights for all, educate the campus community on the history
of the civil rights movement and contemporary social issues encourage the intersection of
academic dialogue and active community engagement, and foster representation for the
diverse communities that comprise Florida State University, including veterans, students with
disabilities, multicultural students, LGBTQ+ students, faith practitioners, environmental rights
advocates, and students across academic disciplines.
This proclamation also reinforces the importance of ensuring that civil rights are not considered
an isolated reference to a historical period or niche interest, but rather as an ongoing
responsibility and resource available to every student. Principal Student Ambassador to the
CRI, Eryn Files, has emphasized strengthening the student-centered nature of the Institute by
prioritizing inclusive and representative events, the establishment of an affiliated RSO that
holds positions for members of the aforementioned diverse communities, facilitated
collaboration with agency leaders who share the needs of their constituents, and the
continuation of community initiatives such as the Selma and Montgomery Civil Rights
Experience, the Unity 5K, and Annual Commemorative MLK week events. These efforts would
further promote civil rights initiatives that serve the diverse communities represented
throughout Florida State University
As representatives of the student body, the Student Senate has an opportunity to recognize
the historical significance of civil rights at Florida State University while encouraging continued
engagement with programs and organizations that promote civic participation, historical
education, leadership development, equal opportunity, and a more inclusive campus
community.
This is not a matter that should receive attention only during Black History Month. Civil rights
should remain a determined commitment of the student body, recognizing the importance of
preserving, honoring, and advancing a legacy that impacts all students and faculty every day
of the year.

seeks to promote informed conversations about breast cancer, encourage individuals to utilize
appropriate screening and preventative resources, and acknowledge the continued efforts of
survivors, caregivers, healthcare providers, and researchers working toward improved
treatments and greater awareness.

February, 6th, 2026
MEMORANDUM #78-001
TO:
Carson Dale, Student Body President
Madeleine Siegel, Student Body Attorney General
Andrew Barrineau, Student Supreme Court Chief Justice
RE: Notice of Non-Compliance - Unauthorized Executive Appointees
This Memorandum serves as formal notice regarding the presence of unauthorized appointees currently
operating within the Executive Branch. The Office of the Senate President issues this notice in good faith, with
the express intent of offering an administrative remedy to restore constitutional order. This notice addresses
several distinct categories of non-compliance discovered during a review of recent Executive Orders and
outlines the necessary steps to regularize the Executive Branch.
It is our preference to rectify these statutory defects collaboratively, thereby avoiding the necessity of further
litigation, Quo Warranto proceedings, or direct intervention by the Judicial Branch.
I. AUTHORITY OF NOTICE
Following the issuance of Advisory Opinion 2025-03, the Student Supreme Court has definitively
ruled that "The President may not fill Cabinet positions without Senate confirmation". The Court
affirmed that Article II, Section 5.1(d) of the Constitution provides "two exclusive avenues" for
appointments: either a two-thirds vote or a majority vote, and that bypassing the Senate is
unconstitutional.
A review of recent Executive Orders reveals a systematic violation of this ruling, relying on the false
premise that "departmental" or "staff" roles are exempt from confirmation. This premise is explicitly
refuted by the Student Body Statutes:
1. Article III, Section 5 of the Student Body Constitution states that membership of the Cabinet
"shall be determined by Statutes".
2.Chapter 301.4(C) of the Student Body Statutes unequivocally states: "Additional internal
department roles may be created by the Secretary or Director, subject to approval from the
Student Body President and Student Senate.”
3.Recent Executive Orders (specifically #80-07, #80-09, and #80-11) explicitly appoint
individuals to "positions within various Executive Departments".
Therefore, under the combined authority of the Student Body Constitution and Chapter 301.4(C),
every individual listed in these orders is a member of the Executive Cabinet.

February, 6th, 2026
MEMORANDUM #78-001
Because these individuals were not submitted for confirmation, they have failed to meet the
condition precedent for office holding required by Chapter 202(4), which states that "duties, rights,
and responsibilities, shall vest [only] upon confirmation by the Student Senate and upon taking the
oath of office". Consequently, these appointees possess no legal authority to act, spend funds, or
execute the laws of the Student Body.
To mitigate liability and prevent the further unauthorized exercise of power, the Senate is issuing
the following directives effective immediately.
II. NOTICE OF SUSPENSION OF EXPIRED "ACTING" APPOINTEES (EO #80-11)
The individuals listed in Executive Order #80-11 (dated December 4, 2025) are hereby noticed as
holding no legal authority to perform official duties effective immediately. Pursuant to SBS
§301.4(b)(4)(C), the authority of an acting officer is strictly limited to a duration of six (6) weeks.
As Executive Order #80-11 was promulgated on December 4, 2025, the statutory window for
acting capacity closed on January 15, 2026. Because no Forwarding Letters were submitted to the
Senate for these individuals, their legal standing terminated by operation of law on that date.
Consequently, any actions taken by these individuals between January 15 and the present are
voidable as they were performed without constitutional or statutory authority.
Appointees Affected:
Ian Seibert (Community Affairs Coordinator)
Isabella LoBianco (Senior Advisor and Special Projects Coordinator)
Jack Rowan (Senior Counselor to the Student Body President and Attorney General)1
Nicolas Valenzuela (Acting Secretary for the Department of Campus Life)
Pursuant to SBS §202.4, §202.3, and §301.4, these individuals shall not produce work product,
authorize expenditures, represent the Student Government Association, or act in any official
capacity. As per SBS §202.4, all duties, rights, and responsibilities of office vest only upon Senate
confirmation and the subsequent administration of the oath of office.
The Senate formally notices that Mr. Jack Rowan’s appointment is constitutionally void ab initio under Article V,
Section 4, which explicitly forbids holding “two major offices... concurrently” by retaining his seat as a COGS
Representative (a constitutionally enumerated Major Office) while attempting to serve as Senior Counselor in the
Executive Office of the President (a Major Office per SBS §100.5(c)(5)).

MEMORANDUM #78-001
III. NOTICE OF INVALID APPOINTMENTS AND INVALIDITY OF EO #80-06
The Office of the Senate President has identified individuals holding titles that have not been
established by the Student Body Statutes nor authorized by a Senate Resolution. Under Article III,
Section 5 of the Constitution, the membership of the Cabinet "shall be determined by Statutes". As
these positions do not exist in law, no individual can validly be appointed to fill them.
Executive Order #80-10 appoints Ms. Urday to the position of "Deputy Solicitor General". In
Student Body Statutes, no such office exists. While this title appears in the proposed text of
Executive Order #80-06, that order is legally void and failed to create the position.2
The Senate understands that Mr. Rubenstein is currently operating under the title of "Deputy
Attorney General", a promotion from his previous confirmed role as Legislative Affairs
Coordinator. The Senate has received no notification, Executive Order, or Forwarding Letter
regarding this change. Unlike the position above, the "Deputy Attorney General" role does not
appear in the Statutes nor in the unratified Executive Order #80-06.
3
Because these offices have not been created by Bill or Resolution, these appointments are
effectively void ab initio. The Senate cannot confirm individuals to positions that do not legally
exist. Therefore, the Senate considers these individuals inactive in these specific capacities:
1.These individuals must immediately return to their previously confirmed roles (if applicable) or
vacate the unauthorized positions.
2.If the Executive Branch wishes to establish these roles, a Bill must be passed to add the position

Executive Order #80-06 explicitly states: "Senate shall adopt this Executive Policy pursuant to Title IV, § 421, upon
which this Executive Policy document shall become effective". No Resolution or Bill was ever introduced or passed to
ratify this order. Consequently, the "Executive Branch Policy" and all positions created solely within it (including

February, 6th, 2026
MEMORANDUM #78-001
IV. NOTICE REGARDING UNCONFIRMED APPOINTEES (EO #80-09 & #80-07)
The Senate has identified approximately twelve (12) individuals currently serving in Executive
Department roles who were appointed solely via Executive Order. This violation concerns
individuals appointed under the following orders: Executive Order #80-07 and Executive Order
#80-09.
These appointments suffer from two distinct legal defects that render the appointees unable to
validly hold office:
1.Under Advisory Opinion 2025-03, the Supreme Court ruled that "The President may not fill
Cabinet positions without Senate confirmation". As Chapter 301.4(C) defines "All roles within
Executive Departments" as members of the Executive Cabinet, the President’s attempt to install
these officers unilaterally via Executive Order violates Article II, Section 5.1(d) of the
Constitution.
2.Many of the specific titles held by these appointees (e.g., Civic Engagement Coordinator,
Social Media Director) do not exist in the Student Body Statutes. They appear to be defined
only within the "Executive Branch Policy" attached to Executive Order #80-06. As established
in Section III, Executive Order #80-06 was never ratified by the Senate as required by its own
text. Therefore, strictly speaking, these specific offices do not legally exist. The President
cannot appoint individuals to positions created by an unratified policy.
The Office of the Senate President recognizes that these positions are intended to serve vital
functions for the Student Body. We desire a cooperative solution to legitimize the Executive Branch
structure.
The Senate is willing to immediately take up a Resolution to:
1.Officially adopt a finalized updated list of Executive Branch departmental positions.
2.Ratify the "Executive Branch Policy" originally proposed in EO #80-06, thereby curing one of
the statutory defects.
However, this legislative cooperation is contingent upon the following:
Ratifying the positions does not automatically ratify the people. Once the Resolution is passed
and the positions legally exist and are correctly advertised to the public, the Executive Branch
must immediately submit a Forwarding Letter containing the names of the individuals up for
Senate confirmation.

February, 6th, 2026
MEMORANDUM #78-001
VI. CONCLUSION
The Student Senate recognizes the ambition and dedication of the Executive Branch in serving the
student body. We understand that the administrative hurdles of governance can often feel
burdensome, and we appreciate the President's desire to staff these departments quickly to deliver
results for the students of Florida State University and to set up statutory precedent for future
administrations to come.
The Office of the Senate President remains committed to meeting with the Executive Branch as
many times as needed during this process. Our goal is to ensure that your administration's priorities
are heard, understood, and represented, so that the Executive Branch is able to faithfully serve the
student body within the framework of our statutes.
It is the position of the Office of the Senate President that true "faithful service" requires adherence
to the law. We are open to future dialogue about reforming the confirmation process to allow for
greater flexibility, but we cannot ignore the current rules while those discussions occur. As the
Supreme Court noted, protecting these processes "protects the separation of powers". We must
ensure that every officer of this government holds their title not by decree, but by the lawful
consent of the governed.
We are a student government of laws, and we must adhere to the Constitution as it stands today.
Furthermore, we must ensure that the Student Body is actually aware of these opportunities. In the
case of recent appointments, positions were created and filled without providing the student body
their legal opportunity to apply. To ensure equity, every vacancy must be properly noticed to the
public as required by Statute. We cannot fast-track appointments at the expense of fair competition
and open access to student government.
We look forward to receiving the forwarded nominations and the updated roster so that we may
move past these procedural defects and return to our mission of representing the student body.
78th Student Senate President
Alexia Holliday

April 6th, 2026
MEMORANDUM #78-002
To: Student Senate
From: Student Senate President
Subject: End of Spring Session Scheduling and Committee Elections Special Session
Pursuant to the governing documents of the Student Government Association, the Senate must
conclude its regular Spring session in accordance with the Student Body Constitution. Article II,
Section 4 of the Constitution provides: “The session of the Senate shall begin on the second week of
classes and terminate on the week prior to the final week of classes, pursuant to the academic
calendar for each semester.” In compliance with this controlling authority, the final regular meeting
of the Spring 2026 Senate session must and will occur on April 15, 2026.
Although the Student Body Statutes have a slightly different schedule, they are subordinate to the
Constitution. Chapter 400: Organization of the Senate states: “The fall, spring, and summer
meetings of the Student Senate shall begin on the second Wednesday in the respective semester and
shall terminate on the Wednesday prior to finals week of the three semesters.” However, the
Constitution supersedes this provision, and therefore the Senate is required to conclude regular
business by the constitutionally mandated date.
At the same time, Statutes explicitly authorize procedural flexibility through special sessions,
further providing that: “The Student Senate President may call a special session of the Senate at
their discretion.” Accordingly, following the conclusion of the regular session on April 15, I will be
calling a Special Session of the 78th Student Senate on April 22, 2026. This session will be limited in
scope for the purpose of electing committee leadership in order to minimize confusion and
leadership turnover between spring, summer, and fall semesters.
Under the Senate Rules of Procedure, committee elections are ordinarily conducted following
Inauguration. Rule Five: Committees states: “Committee elections shall occur immediately after
the reading of committee assignments following fall and spring inaugurations. Senate shall move to
enter committee caucus for the purpose of electing Committee Chairs and Vice-Chairs.” Because
Inauguration will occur on April 24, after the constitutionally required conclusion of the regular
session, strict adherence to this timing is not feasible within the regular meeting framework as it
stands. As such, the April 22 Special Session will function as an interim mechanism to conduct
committee elections in advance of the Summer term due to these extenuating special circumstances.

sections.text:
April 6th, 2026
MEMORANDUM #78-002
To ensure both continuity and procedural legitimacy, the elections conducted during the April 22
Special Session will include participation from Spring Senators-elect; however, because these
members will not yet be sworn in due to how late Inauguration is this semester, the results of these
elections must be formally ratified by the Senate at the first meeting of the Summer Session after
Inauguration has occurred. Under guidance from Student Governance and Advocacy, this
ratification will occur through a consent item on the May 20 agenda, thereby ensuring that
committee leadership is ultimately confirmed by a properly constituted and sworn Senate in
accordance with governing rules. As a reminder, any senators elected into committee leadership in
spring that take a summer leave of absence will automatically resume their post upon the
reconvening of Senate in fall.
In preparation for the April 22 Special Session, committee assignments will be issued following
New Senator Orientation on the April 15 so that all participating members are adequately
informed and placed prior to the election process. This adjusted sequencing ensures that the intent
of Rule Five, namely, that elections occur after members are assigned to committees and able to
deliberate within those bodies, is preserved as best as possible given the timeline and scheduling of
Inauguration this year.
Finally, it is important to note that any legislation still in the legislative process following the April

MEMORANDUM #78-003
To: Student Senate
From: Student Senate President
Subject: Creation of New Senate Officer Team Positions
I. PURPOSE
This memorandum formally establishes five (5) new positions within the Office of the Senate
President: a Bill Drafter, Assistant Clerk, Assistant Historian(s), Digital Media Officer, and
Technology Officer. These positions are created pursuant to the authority of the Senate
President and in accordance with the Senate Rules of Procedure, per Rule 2.6. These
creation of these new positions is a deliberate effort to balance workload across the officer
team and elevate the Senate's operational capacity.
II. BACKGROUND & RATIONALE
As the legislative demands of the Student Senate continue to arise, it has become necessary
to formalize and distribute specific responsibilities currently managed and absorbed by
existing officers. Each of the positions established herein addresses its own operational need
within the chamber and is grounded in pre-existing duties for other positions per Chapter
400. of Student Body Statutes.
III. NEW POSITIONS ESTABLISHED
Bill Drafter
The Bill Drafter shall operate under the direction of the Clerk and shall serve as the primary
technical writing resource for the Student Senate. The duties of the Bill Drafter shall
include, but are not limited to:
Assisting Senators in the technical writing, formatting, and drafting of legislation to
ensure compliance with Student Body Statutes, Senate Rules of Procedure, and
provided Senate formatting guidelines;
Proactively collaborating with Senators on the drafting of legislation prior to formal
submission; and
Receiving all legislation submitted by Senators, ensuring proper preparation and
formatting, before transmitting such legislation to the Clerk for inclusion on the weekly
agenda.

JUNE 18th, 2026
MEMORANDUM #78-003
Assistant Clerk
The Assistant Clerk shall operate under the direction of the Clerk and shall assist in
tracking legislation and executing administrative duties within the Chamber. The duties of
the Assistant Clerk shall include, but are not limited to:
Serving as the primary officer responsible for managing and compiling all standing
committee agendas and committee agenda packets, as well as the agendas for any ad
hoc committees and college delegation meetings while ensuring their postage at least 24
hours in advance of their respective meetings;
Tracking and managing all amendments passed in committee, as well as any
amendments submitted by Senators prior to being heard on the Senate floor or in

in taking official minutes during full Senate sessions. The duties of the Assistant Historian(s)

Taking, formatting, and finalizing all minutes for standing committee meetings, ad hoc
committee meetings, and college delegation meetings; and
Ensuring that all completed committee and delegation minutes are properly compiled
and added to the weekly Senate Agenda for formal approval, with all such minutes
uploaded to CivicPlus within twenty-four (24) hours of their respective meetings.
Digital Media Officer
The Digital Media Officer shall operate under the direction of the Public Affairs Officer and
shall assist in maintaining the Senate's digital communications and outreach presence. The
duties of the Digital Media Officer shall include, but are not limited to:
Maintaining the Senate's social media presence via Instagram, LinkedIn, and any other
platform deemed necessary by the Senate President;
Creating and executing a comprehensive monthly content calendar encompassing all
digital platforms and outreach efforts.

JUNE 18th, 2026
MEMORANDUM #78-003
Technology Officer
The Technology Officer shall serve as the primary technology administrator for the Student
Senate, responsible for the overarching management, maintenance, and oversight of all
digital infrastructure and physical technical equipment utilized by the legislative branch.
The duties of the Technology Officer shall include, but are not limited to:
Managing the administration of all official Student Senate email accounts, including
those assigned to Senate Officers and standing committees;
Generating virtual Zoom links for all legislative proceedings and managing the creation
and administration of all official Student Senate Qualtrics forms;
Managing CivicPlus training, technical troubleshooting, and permissions for Senators;
Serving as the CivicPlus Zoom recording and camera operator during Senate sessions
and providing technical support during standing committee meetings when requested;
Maintaining a comprehensive technical manual for the Senate while acting as the
primary liaison to the SGA Webmaster for website updates; and
Ensuring that every Senate meeting, standing committee meeting, ad hoc committee
meeting, and college delegation meeting is actively recorded via Zoom, with resulting
recordings immediately uploaded to CivicPlus for public record following adjournment.
IV. EFFECTIVE DATE
The positions established herein shall take effect immediately upon the issuance of this
memorandum. All appointments to these positions will be made by the Senate President in
accordance with Chapter 400 of Student Body Statutes and shall be confirmed by the Senate
upon their selection.
V. CONCLUSION
The establishment of these five positions reflects the continued growth and
professionalization of the Student Senate. Each role has been carefully designed to address
specific operational needs and while ensuring Senate can fulfill its legislative responsibilities
with the highest degree of professionalism and efficiency. Questions regarding this
memorandum may be directed to the Office of the Senate President.
Respectfully,
78th Student Senate President
Alexia Holliday

77th STUDENT SENATE
Legislation Cover Sheet
Senate Bill/Resolution/Proclamation/PCA #: 005
Primary Sponsor(s): Cruz, Noumena
Co-sponsor(s): Brown, Lalani
Short Title: Title VII Reform: Comprehensive Amendments to the Elections Code
Summary of Legislation:
This legislation overhauls Title VII, the Elections Code, to enhance transparency,
accountability, and fairness in elections. Key provisions include replacing the campaign
materials approval system with an online public registry, revising financial disclosure
requirements, codifying processes for handling violations, halving campaign spending limits,
and altering debate and timeline procedures. Other changes and explanations for each
amendment can be found in attachment 1.
Background Information:
An election system must be clear, robust, replicable, and democratic. Unfortunately, the
current Elections Code falls short of meeting these standards. The Elections Commission lacks
key due process mechanisms, creating potential for inconsistent or unfair rulings. Loopholes in
the code enable systematic fraud. Basic errors, including typos, render some sections
unenforceable, while candidates frequently encounter unnecessary bureaucratic hurdles.
Incremental edits made over recent years have only deepened these systemic flaws. This
legislation represents the culmination of months of collaboration with members from every
branch of Student Government, addressing these issues comprehensively to build a functional,
transparent, and fair election system.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
This legislation implements a comprehensive overhaul of Title VII, the Elections Code,
introducing several major reforms to enhance transparency, accountability, and fairness in the
election process. Key provisions establish an online public registry for campaign materials,
requiring candidates and parties to submit materials for public disclosure with standardized
disclaimers; this registry eliminates the prior approval system, streamlining compliance while
improving transparency. The bill codifies processes for handling violations, emphasizing due
process by instituting clearer mechanisms for penalty assignments, default judgments for
unexcused absences at hearings, increasing reporting requirements from the Supervisor, and
restructuring point penalties. Financial disclosure requirements are revised to improve clarity
and efficiency, reducing confusion for candidates while ensuring accurate reporting and
enforcement. Campaign spending limits are halved. Debate and timeline procedures are
altered to make fall debates optional while increasing public participation opportunities for
spring debates. The bill contains several other provisions designed to further strengthen
transparency, accountability, and fairness in the election process.Docusign Envelope ID: 40C86981-F852-425F-B2EE-75BB444822FC

Short Title: New Senate Legislation and Funding Legislation Deadline(s)
Summary of Legislation:
This bill amends the legislation submission process for all forms of legislation, requiring that
they be submitted through a Qualtrics form hosted by the SGA Webmaster no later than Friday
at midnight before the upcoming Senate meeting. It also establishes the protocol for submitting
Funding Board Legislation, mandating that such legislation be submitted by Thursday at
midnight following passage in the respective funding board and approval by the Finance
Committee, with the Finance Committee Chair responsible for submitting it for Second
Reading.
Background Information:
In previous history, the due date set for Senate Legislation, Tuesday at Noon, was changed
from Monday at Noon during the 2024 Summer Student Senate Legislative Session. Since
then, the due date has been difficult and unattainable to abide by. Therefore, the new dates
will provide efficiency for the development of the Senate Calendar.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
Funding boards (RTAC, PAC, and Finance) will be required to submit legislation on the
Thursday before the upcoming Senate meeting by midnight. Additionally, Senators will be
required to submit legislation on the Friday before the upcoming Senate meeting by midnight.

Short Title: Amending Chapter 807 to Revise Funding Request Deadlines for RSOs
Summary of Legislation: This bill amends Chapter 807 of the Student Body Statutes to
extend the timeline for Recognized Student Organizations (RSOs) to submit funding requests.
Specifically, it increases the required timeline for PAC funding requests from 21 to 30 school
days prior to an event or activity. This change accounts for delays caused by the Senate’s new
approval timelines, ensuring that RSOs receive funding in a timely manner.
Background Information:
In our current Senate administration, changes in the timeline for Senate approval of funding
requests have led to delays in the disbursement of funds to Recognized Student Organizations
(RSOs). As the approval process timeline extends by an additional seven days after the initial
review by the Programming Allocations Committee (PAC), many RSOs have experienced
delays that jeopardize their ability to execute events and programs effectively. Currently, PAC
funding requests must be submitted at least 21 school days prior to an event. However, due to
the extended review and approval timeline of Senate, this deadline no longer provides
sufficient time for funds to be received before the planned activities. The proposed amendment
extends the PAC deadline to 30 school days to allow for sufficient time for funding approval,
addressing the delays and ensuring that RSOs have the financial resources they need well in
advance of their events.
Student organizations across campus rely on timely funding to host events that enrich campus
life and facilitate professional development. Delayed funding not only disrupts event planning
but also undermines the ability of RSOs to fulfill their mission and engage with their members
effectively. By aligning the PAC deadline with the RTAC deadline, this amendment streamlines
the process and mitigates the adverse effects caused by prolonged approval times.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:

Short Title: Repeal of the Civic Engagement Board
Summary of Legislation:
This bill would repeal all legislation pertaining to the Civic Engagement Board, ending its status
as an affiliated project.
Background Information:
The Civic Engagement Board has been an affiliated project of the Student Government
Association for over the past year. During this time, its noble organizational goals have
overlapped with related entities, both internally within SGA and externally within the College of
Social Sciences and Public Policy. As SGA continues to undergo significant structural reforms-
particularly in re-evaluating the roles and relevance of its affiliated projects, bureaus and other
boards- it would be in the association’s best interest to repeal CEB’s designation as an
affiliated project. In the future, efforts for a more streamlined, clearly defined, and non-
overlapping organizational framework can be created along with the rest of the executive
changes.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
This would remove the Civic Engagement Board as an affiliated project of Student
Government. The Board would retain RSO status and autonomous operations, independent of
SGA. It would be the first step in a series of internal changes redefining the current operational
functions of SGA.

Short Title:
Campaign Finance Transparency Act of 2025
Summary of Legislation:
This bill amends Chapters 701 and 709 of the Student Body Statutes to clarify the definition
and required components of Final Expense Statements. It expands financial documentation
requirements and mandates submission of a Financial Recap Summary for political parties.
Background Information:
Final Expense Statements are essential for ensuring financial transparency during Student
Government elections. However, ambiguity surrounding required documentation has led to
inconsistent reporting and oversight. This legislation was drafted in response to concerns
raised by the Office of Elections and student organizations regarding financial accountability. It
seeks to create a more structured and enforceable standard for campaign finance reporting.

financial records, including itemized expenses, donor reports, and a verified Financial Recap
Summary. This would be for the entire year after the election season as well. It standardizes
the required documentation and aligns submission expectations with templates provided by the
Supervisor of Elections, ensuring consistency and transparency in the electoral process.

Short Title: A Resolution Congratulating the Student Body President on Being Elected Chair
of the Florida Student Association and Proposing a Revision to Chapter 607, Student Body
Statutes
Summary of Legislation:
The resolution congratulates President Carson Dale on his election as Chair of the Florida
Student Association and proposes an amendment to Chapter 607, Student Body Statutes,
designating the COGS Speaker as FSU’s representative on the Florida Student Association’s
Graduate Student Committee.
Background Information:
The Florida Student Association (FSA) is the official nonprofit organization representing the
more than 400,000 students in the Florida State University System.1 The FSA’s board of
directors is made up of the student body presidents of the twelve state universities, who elect a
chair from among themselves.2 The chair of the FSA serves as a member of the Florida State
University System Board of Governors, which regulates the entire Florida State University
System.
On May 30, 2025, FSU Student Body President Carson Dale was elected Chair of the FSA by
the FSA Board of Directors. In consultation with Speaker Rowan, President Dale proposed an
amendment to the FSA constitution that created a Graduate Student Committee, comprised of
a graduate student representative from each of the twelve state universities. The amendment
was adopted by the Board of Directors. As a result, FSU SGA needs to designate, by statute,
an official to serve on the Graduate Student Committee.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
The resolution congratulates President Carson Dale on his election as Chair of the FSA.
Additionally, the resolution proposes an amendment to Chapter 607, Student Body Statutes,
which governs COGS. Per § 607.1(d)(1), SBS, COGS may directly propose legislation to
Senate. When COGS proposes legislation, the legislation must be introduced by the Senate
President or the Senate Judiciary Committee.

Short Title: An Amendment to Chapter 702, Chapter 705(1), and Chapter 712: ACCESS
(“Advancing Convenience and Comprehensive Electoral Scheduling”) Act
Summary of Legislation:
The aim of this bill is to make amendments to establish an extended polling period and modify
the date of the debate. General Elections shall now take place from a Monday to a Tuesday,
where online polls are open from 8:00AM to 8:00PM both days. The results of the election will
be announced prior to 11:00PM on the second day of the elections (Tuesday). The debate
must also take place during the nine (9)-day campaign period.
Background Information:
Upon the results of the election poll question regarding extending polling hours, which was
favored by the population of FSU students who votes, this bill executes this want voiced by the
Student Body. It also ensures the schedule is logistical, maintainable, and can accommodate
the various schedules of candidates and members of SGA parties. It also streamlines the
schedule so that it is clear in statutes.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
This bill establishes the eighth Monday and the following Tuesday of the semester as the
election days. Polls will be open online from 8AM-8PM on both Monday and Tuesday. This
makes it a full twenty-four (24) hour window between both days for students to vote for their
representatives. Campaigning is prohibited prior to 12:00AM on the Monday one week before
the first day of elections. The Supervisor of Elections (SOE) shall announce the results prior to
11:00PM on the second day of elections/open polls. The method of this announcement shall
be up to the SOE. The debate for spring elections shall occur during the nine (9) – day
campaign period.

Summary of Legislation:
The Executive Departments Act of 2025 aims to set a precedent for future Executive cabinets
to create a comprehensive framework for the execution of policy projects and the improvement
of Florida State University’s campus. It defines positions with the Executive
Departments/Cabinet, reorganizes entities into other categories, and streamlines legislation
pertaining to appendages of the executive branch.
Background Information:
The Dale - Ramirez-Romero – Wyatt administration developed a framework for an outline of
am Executive cabinet during the Spring 2025 semester. After communication with Senate
leadership, a working group was formed to codify the executive cabinet into statutory
language.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
The Executive Departments Act of 2025 amends major offices, outlines the Executive
Departments, and renumbers certain SGA entities into Affiliated Projects.

Short Title: Reclassifying the Inter-Residence Hall Council as an Affiliated Project under Title
XI
Summary of Legislation:
This resolution reclassifies the Inter-Residence Hall Council (IRHC) from an Executive Bureau
under Chapter 907 of the Student Body Statutes to an Affiliated Project under a newly created
Title XI. The change reflects IRHC’s operational autonomy while maintaining its ability to
request funding and serve students effectively.
Background Information:
The Executive Branch has undertaken a restructuring initiative aimed at dissolving Executive
Bureaus and clarifying the organizational structure of affiliated entities. The Inter-Residence
Hall Council, which has long functioned with significant independence and direct community
engagement, meets the criteria outlined in the statutes for an Affiliated Project. This
reclassification was discussed in consultation with key stakeholders, including IRHC leadership
and members of the Executive Branch. As an organization that provides vital programming,
advocacy, and leadership opportunities for residential students, this transition aligns IRHC
more closely with its current structure and mission.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
If enacted, this legislation will formally remove IRHC from Chapter 907 of the Student Body
Statutes and establish a new Title XI to house Affiliated Projects, beginning with the IRHC.
This will not impact IRHC’s daily operations, leadership, or programming, but will provide it with
formal recognition as an autonomous entity. The resolution also ensures that IRHC retains
access to funding through the Senate and other SGA resources while reflecting the
organization’s unique operational role outside of the Executive Branch.

Short Title: Amending Chapter 1005 to update the name of the Hispanic/Latinx Student Union
to Hispanic/Latine Student Union.
Summary of Legislation:
This bill would amend Chapter 1005 of the Student Body Statutes to update the name of the
Hispanic/Latinx Student Union to Hispanic/Latine Student Union. The bill makes technical edits
by striking the letter “x” and replacing it with “e” to reflect evolving language preferences within
the community.
Background Information:
The proposed name change from “Hispanic/Latinx Student Union” to “Hispanic/Latine Student
Union” reflects a broader movement within academic institutions and student organizations to
adopt more inclusive and culturally accurate language. The term "Latine" has gained traction
as a gender-neutral alternative to "Latino" or "Latina" that aligns more naturally with Spanish
linguistic rules, making it easier to pronounce and more accessible to native Spanish speakers.
Unlike Latinx, which often relies on English phonetics and has been criticized for being difficult
to vocalize in Spanish, Latine is viewed by many students, scholars, and community advocates
as a more authentic and inclusive expression of pan-ethnic identity.
Multiple universities across the United States have already adopted the term Latine in the
names of their student organizations, cultural centers, and programming. For example, the
University of California, Berkeley uses “Latine Student Union,” and institutions like Brown
University and the University of Oregon regularly incorporate the term into their heritage month
programming and identity-based support services. Notably, the University of Florida (UF) has
officially renamed its Hispanic Student Association to the Hispanic-Latine Student Association,
and its campus-wide events, including the annual Hispanic-Latine Student Assembly,
consistently use Latine in all branding and communications. UF’s successful adoption of the
term in both student life and university-level engagement demonstrates that this shift is both
feasible and positively received within a large Florida-based institution.

Short Title: The SGA External Transparency and Digital Records Act
Summary of Legislation:
This bill repeals and replaces Chapter 210 of the Student Body Statutes to establish the “SGA
Digital Records Act of 2025.” It creates comprehensive standards for publishing, preserving,
and managing all digital records, websites, and social media under SGA. It aims to strengthen
transparency, ensure compliance with public records laws, and safeguard institutional memory.
Background Information:
Chapter 210, first enacted as the SGA Website Act of 2007, no longer adequately addresses
modern digital operations, multi-platform communication, or compliance with Florida Sunshine
and SGA Public Records laws. As SGA has expanded its online presence, clearer standards
are needed for official records, archives, websites, and social media to avoid inconsistent
practices and data loss. This legislation was developed through review of current statutory
gaps. It also aligns with trends in peer institutions’ digital governance.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
If enacted, this legislation will formally codify the platforms and standards for SGA websites,
CivicPlus, Municode, and official social media, defining publication timelines, branding
requirements, credential protocols, and enforcement mechanisms. It will enhance transparency
by requiring timely posting of records and protecting digital continuity during officer transitions,
with remedies for violations including judicial enforcement.

77th STUDENT SENATE
Legislation Cover Sheet
Senate Bill/Resolution #: Bill #77-034 and Resolution #77-060
Primary Sponsor(s): Goldstein, Rios
Co-sponsor(s): Add any Co-Sponsors here
Short Title: Establishment of New Student Organization Funding Programs and Operating
Policies & Procedures
Summary of Legislation:
Bill #77-034 creates two new student organization funding programs in the Student Body
Statutes: the RSO Allocation Committee and the RSO Development Fund. It also repeals
outdated provisions and refines the Statutes to streamline the allocation of A&S fees. The
accompanying Resolution #77-060 formally adopts operational policies and procedures for the
RSO Allocation Committee, including funding guidelines, meeting structure, and evaluation
criteria.
Background Information:
In recent years, SGA and the Department of Student Engagement have received feedback
from Recognized Student Organizations (RSOs) on campus indicating that RSOs have faced
obstacles in accessing student government funding due to duplicative, outdated, and overly
complex policies.
The Student Senate has recognized the need to restructure and simplify the process to
promote accessibility, equity, and efficiency; the FY 2025-26 SGA budget adopted by the
Student Senate contemplates eliminating the Programming Allocation Committee (PAC), the
Resource for Travel Allocation Committee (RTAC), the Organizational Fund, and the RSO
Budget Fund and replacing those funding programs with a more consolidated, streamlined
funding process that will reduce confusion and provide a “one-stop shop” for RSOs to seek
funding from SGA.
This legislation is the product of collaboration between the Student Senate, the SGA Executive
Branch, the Department of Student Engagement, and campus partners and reflects best
practices for financial governance and student engagement.Docusign Envelope ID: 6EC0BA51-9D81-4FC0-B77B-FD6D09FCE19B

sections.heading: Page 2
sections.text:
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
If enacted, this legislation will:
• Establish the RSO Allocation Committee (RSOAC) to centralize and standardize
supplemental funding for undergraduate RSOs;
• Establish elections for members of the RSO Allocation Committee to increase
transparency, democratic participation, and student voice in the allocation of A&S fees;
• Create the RSO Development Fund, providing small grants to support new and
developing RSOs;
• Repeal outdated chapters (e.g., Chapters 807 and 815) and replace them with a more
robust and efficient framework for allocating SGA funding to RSOs;
• Clarify funding eligibility, limitations, and approval processes;
• Adopt a transparent and merit-based rubric to guide allocation decisions;
• Improve communication of funding opportunities through required social media
outreach; and
• Enhance transparency in SGA’s funding allocation process and ensure that these
programs are evaluated regularly to identify recommendations for further program
enhancement in the future.
Ultimately, this legislation will enhance accountability, transparency, and equitable access to
funding for student organizations.

Short Title: Guiding Oversight of Legislative Disbursements Act of 2025
Summary of Legislation: This bill consolidates and restructures the financial governance
framework of the Student Senate by amending multiple chapters of the Student Body Statutes.
It eliminates the Senate Budget Committee as a standing body, reassigns oversight to the
Finance Committee, and updates procedures for budget amendments, transfers, reserve
accounts, and fund usage. The legislation establishes a standardized project proposal process
for CAD Fund requests and revises thresholds for Senate Projects and other allocations.
Background Information: The Student Senate’s fiscal process has long been divided
between overlapping committees, leading to inefficiencies, confusion, and limited
transparency. The bill draws from best practices in financial oversight to clarify committee
roles, streamline review procedures, and improve long-term fiscal stewardship of Activity &
Service (A&S) Fees. It also strengthens accountability by introducing new statutory
requirements, including a standardized proposal form and revised voting thresholds for major
allocations.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
The legislation centralizes fiscal responsibilities under the Finance Committee, establishes
clearer budget amendment processes, and revises procedures across the Budget Act, Senate
Projects, CAD Fund, CLC Funding, and Reserve Account statutes. It modernizes and
normalizes Senate financial operations, ensuring more consistent oversight, stronger
accountability, and greater efficiency in the allocation of A&S Fees.

77th STUDENT SENATE
Legislation Cover Sheet
Senate Bill #: 051
Primary Sponsor(s): Goldstein, LoBianco
Co-sponsor(s):
Short Title: Amending the Student Body Statutes to Establish Procedures for the
Organizational Session and Create Oaths of Office for the Senate President and Senate
President Pro Tempore
Summary of Legislation:
This bill amends Chapter 400 of the Student Body Statutes to codify the Organizational
Session of the Student Senate pursuant to the newly amended Student Body Constitution, and
creates new Sections 202.9 through 202.10 establishing distinct Oaths of Office for the Senate
President and Senate President Pro Tempore. The bill defines the Dean of the Senate’s role,
outlines the timing, certification, and ratification of the Organizational Session, and ensures the
statutory framework aligns with the new constitutional requirements.
Background Information:
Following the 2025 constitutional amendment to Article II, Section 4, the Student Senate is
now required to convene an Organizational Session before each new term to elect its presiding
officers. The current Student Body Statutes do not provide procedures for this session, nor
distinct oaths for the Senate’s leadership positions. This bill establishes those provisions to
provide clarity, transparency, and continuity of governance. It also re-introduces the Dean of
the Senate, still defined as the most senior, concurrently serving Senator not returning to the
next Senate, as the neutral presiding officer for the Organizational Session. These reforms
were drafted to modernize Senate transitions, prevent procedural uncertainty.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
1. Add 400.8 to create the statutory framework for the Organizational Session, including
timing, presiding officer, quorum, voting, oath administration, and certification.
2. Add 202.9–202.10 to establish distinct oaths for the Senate President and Senate
President Pro Tempore and to assign the Dean of the Senate as the official to
administer those oaths.
3. Update cross-references within Chapter 400 to reflect these changes.
Together, these updates align statute with the amended Constitution, ensure fair and
transparent leadership elections, and strengthen the ethical and institutional framework
of the Student Senate.Docusign Envelope ID: AC6C724C-AA43-4B2B-A77F-1001287A47D6

Short Title: Adopting the Annual Student Government Association Budget for Fiscal Year

Summary of Legislation:
This bill established the Activity & Service (A&S) Fee Budget for the 2025-2026 fiscal year,
totaling $15,391,628. It outlines the allocation of these funds among the Student Sente,
Congress of Graduate Students (COGS), and the Division of Student Affairs (DSA) for student
engagement, Union operations, and Campus Recreation.
Background Information:
The A&S Fee budget is a fundamental component of student government funding, supporting
student organizations, leadership initiatives, and university services. This allocation ensures
continued access to student resources, programming, and operational support. The budget
process follows the Florida State University Body Statutes and is subject to approval by the
77th Student Senate.
This will be the inaugural year we recognize the annual Activity & Service (A&S) Fee Budget
as Senate Bill 1851.

I. General
A. No A&S funded account may pay any stipend, wage, salary, or salary increase to
any positions not funded in the FY 2025-2026 Budget without express consent of
the Student Senate in the form of a bill or resolution, except as may be funded in
the COGS FY 2025-2026 Budget.
B. In the event of shortfalls or excesses of entities funded in this budget, the Vice
President of Student Affairs, the SGA Advisor, the Senate President, and the
Student Body President shall meet to review options. The COGS Speaker shall
be invited when the shortfall involves entities funded by COGS. No decisions
shall be made without a majority vote of the Student Senate.
C. The FY 2025-2026 Budget was created under the current $12.86 per credit hour
A&S Fee. Should the FSU Board of Trustees approve an increase to the A&S
Fee, the Student Senate Budget Committee should reconvene to allocate any
additional projected funds for the remainder of the fiscal year.
D. The FY 2025-2026 Budget was created under the terms of a Memorandum of
Understanding (“MOU”) among the FSU Division of Finance and Administration,
the Division of Student Affairs, and the Student Government Association, as
approved by the 76th Student Senate in Resolution 33. The Budget Committee,
and the Student Senate as a whole, intend to fully comply with the MOU and are
of the opinion that any proviso language regarding the covered entities help
ensure quality of service and compliance with various state and university
policies, rather than non-compliance with the MOU.
E. Monies allocated in the Food category shall be held in compliance with Student
Body Statute § 803.7(A) which states “No SGA branch, office, agency, bureau, or
affiliated project shall be allocated more than fifteen percent (15%) of its annual
budget in the Food category.”
F. Any and all budgeted organizations found in violation of Student Body Statutes
shall be subject to the appropriate sanctions contained in the Finance Code and
recommended by the Finance Committee, the Budget Committee, and the
Student Senate.
G. It is the position of the Budget Committee and the Student Senate that the
current organization for the Student Government Association is no longer
providing students with the value that should come with such a large budget.
Therefore, the Senate shall enact statutory changes to reorganize the Student
Government Association in accordance with the funding structure laid out in the
FY 2025-2026 Budget.
1. In order to ensure accountability and responsibility within SGA entities,
the Senate shall introduce legislation converting executive bureaus into
departments under the Executive Branch that, either directly or through
an Executive officer who the Student Body President has ultimate
responsibility for, report to the Student Body President or redesignating
executive bureaus sufficiently affiliated with a university entity (such as
MHC) to an Affiliated Project. The legislation shall redesignate the Office
of Governmental Affairs as the Department of External Affairs.

unique circumstances, the Senate shall introduce legislation
redesignating the Homecoming Executive Council as an Affiliated

programming, the Senate shall introduce legislation making the Class

designee, and reorienting their responsibilities towards certain signature
SGA events, as well as recurring programming.
5. In order to ensure that all Student Organizations have a fair chance to
receive SGA funding, the Senate shall introduce legislation restructuring
the PAC, RTAC, and RSO Budget Fund process by creating a student
organization Grant system where qualifying Student Organizations may
receive a set amount of SGA funds on a first come, first serve, basis as

I. SGA shall be authorized to enter into funding agreements with other University
partners for the implementation of the FY 2025-26 budget, subject to approval by
the Vice President for Student Affairs.
J. The Student Body Treasurer shall, within 10 school days of the effective date of
this bill, provide a written memorandum to each budgeted entity detailing the
allocated budget and any proviso language on said allocation.

A. It is the position of the 77th Student Senate that the Bobby E. Leach Student
Recreation Center, the Fitness and Movement Clinic, the Intramural fields, the
Rez Lakefront Park and Retreat Center, and the Rec SportsPlex have been
primarily funded by student dollars and that these facilities' primary purpose is for

various buildings and programs across campus, has been funded by student
dollars and that these facilities' primary purpose is for supporting the student
experience.
B. Any A&S-Funded event or entertainment provided by the Union shall be free and
open to all students with valid identification. Non-FSU students shall be subject to
admission fees.

Whereas: Native American Heritage Month has been celebrated every November since its
designation by the United States Congress following House Joint Resolution 577 being signed
into action on June 26, 1990, and
Whereas: as stated by the United States Department of the Interior, Native American Heritage
Month is designated as a time to celebrate the traditions, languages, and stories of Native
American and Alaska Native communities to ensure their rich histories and contributions
continue to thrive with each passing generation, and
Whereas: Florida State University (FSU) has built a long-lasting relationship with the Seminole
Tribe in an effort to preserve their values and honor their heritage, and
Whereas: Native American Heritage Month offers a chance to inform and educate students on
the unique history and resilience of Native Americans, as well as to recognize past injustices
that have burdened these communities, and
Whereas: on November 1st and 2nd, four Student Senators- Matthew Boudreau, Alexia
Holliday, Ashley Wong, and Jonus Goldstein- were a part of the first group of FSU students in
history to volunteer with the Seminole Tribe of Florida at their annual American Indigenous Arts
Celebration (AIAC) presented by the Ah-Tah-Thi-Ki Museum on the Big Cypress Reservation,
and
Whereas: the Student Senate shall strive to foster opportunities for such engagement and
service with the Seminole Tribe of Florida, and in the past has recognized federal holidays
acknowledging, celebrating, and honoring Native American and Indigenous communities, and
shall continue to do so, and
Whereas: the Native American and Indigenous Studies Center, established in 2023, is an
invaluable entity on campus that continues to uphold its mission statement to further community
engagement in Native American and Indigenous research and artistic practice, and
Be it resolved by the Seventy-sixth Student Senate at Florida State University that: the
Student Senate formally recognizes Native American Heritage Month and supports NativeDocusign Envelope ID: 7CDC1EBB-D860-4F5D-A0DC-6481DE94806A

and their contributions and relations to FSU.

Resolution #: 03
Primary Sponsor(s): LoBianco, Tully
Co-Sponsor(s): Goldstein
Date: December 4th, 2024
Whereas: There is an amendment that could be made to the Senate Rules of Procedure to
update the document with a more efficient way to operate out Senate Officer team, and
Whereas: Student Body Statute §401.1 states, “Changes to the Rules of Procedure must be
done through resolution and adopted by a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the Senate,” therefore
Be it resolved by the Seventy-seventh Student Senate at Florida State University that:
The following amendments to Rule Four of the Student Senate Rules of Procedure are adopted
as outlined in the amended text below:
1. The Student Senate President shall be responsible for the duties of all vacant Senate
Officers.
2. The Parliamentarian shall advise the Senate on matters of procedure and pertinent laws,
statutes, and constitutional provisions and enforce the rules relating to procedure. The
Parliamentarian shall maintain order in the Senate Chambers under the direction of the
President or other presiding officer(s). The Parliamentarian shall strictly enforce the rules
relating to conduct within the Senate Chambers. The Parliamentarian shall perform any
other duties that the President shall determine to be necessary.
3. The Press Secretary Public Affairs Officer shall be responsible for maintaining the
Senate social media presence and outreach. The Press Secretary Public Affairs Officer
shall work with committee chairs to help inform the student body on committee meeting
information. The Press Secretary Public Affairs Officer shall also perform any other
duties that the Student Senate President or President Pro-Tempore shall determine to
be necessary for these purposes.
1. The Press Secretary Public Affairs Officer shall be in contact with the SGA
Webmaster to ensure that postings are within the Florida State University
communications guidelines.
2. The Senate Press Secretary Public Affairs Officer shall post on the Student
Senate Instagram account at the beginning of the fall and spring semesters when
PAC, RTAC, and all relevant funding board requests open. This post should
include a brief description of the funding boards, links to the funding board pages
on the SGA website, and links to the applications. The Student Senate Press
Secretary Public Affairs Officer shall also contact the Executive Branch when the
post is up, so a post can be made on the SGA Instagram account.
4. The Senate Clerk shall be responsible for tracking and distributing legislation and other
literature to Senators. The Clerk shall also work in collaboration with the Historian to
create and maintain the weekly Senate agenda. The Clerk shall be responsible forDocusign Envelope ID: 5839255E-134F-4467-A9AE-0A54384ADC73

sections.heading: Page 2
sections.text:
managing the CivicPlus application during sessions of the Senate. The Clerk shall also
perform any other duties that the Senate President or President Pro-Tempore shall
determine to be necessary.
5. The Senate Historian shall be responsible for taking minutes in the Senate Chamber.
The Historian shall also work in collaboration with the Clerk to create and maintain the
weekly Senate agenda. The Historian shall also perform any other duties that the Senate
President or President Pro-Tempore shall determine to be necessary.
6. The Senate Chief of Staff shall be responsible for managing the deadlines and
responsibilities of the Senate Parliamentarian, Press Secretary, Clerk, and Historian.
The Chief of Staff shall also be in discussions with the Senate President and President
Pro-Tempore regarding any ambitions they hope to accomplish during their terms. The
Chief of Staff shall also perform any other duties that the Senate President or president
Pro-Tempore shall determine to be necessary.
7. The Parliamentarian, Press Secretary Public Affairs Officer, Historian, Clerk, Chief of
Staff, and any additional appointed legislative officers shall be appointed by the
President from outside the membership of the Senate and shall be subject to
confirmation from the Senate.
Be it further resolved that: Any other mention of Senate Press Secretary in the Rules of
Procedure shall be updated to Senate Public Affairs Officer, and any mention of Senate Chief of
Staff shall be removed entirely.

Whereas: Chapter 815, Student Body Statutes establishes a “Recognized Student Organization
(RSO) Budget Fund” to provide financial support for operational expenses and event planning,
creating a stable budget for otherwise independent Recognized Student Organizations; and
Whereas: The FY 2024-25 SGA Budget included an allocation of $150,000 for the RSO Budget
Fund; and
Whereas: The RSO Budget Fund Committee opened an application window on October 25,
2024, through November 1, 2024, to receive funding applications from RSOs on campus; and
Whereas: The Committee leadership and Student Body Treasurer’s office evaluated all of the
applications received and developed a list of recommended funding allocations reflecting the
most effective and efficient use of this funding, which was presented to the Student Senate
Budget Committee for consideration at its December 2, 2024, meeting; and
Whereas: The Student Senate Budget Committee met on December 2, 2024, to consider this
list of recommended allocations and made several amendments to best meet the needs of the
student organizations on campus and the Florida State University student body.
Be it resolved by the Seventy-seventh Student Senate at Florida State University that:
Allocations from the RSO Budget Fund are made for FY 2024-25 as provided in Attachment #1
to this Resolution.
Be it further resolved that: In order to best support student activities on campus, the
remaining balance of $13,649.74 from the RSO Budget Fund shall be reallocated to the
Resource for Travel Allocations Committee (RTAC) for the remainder of Fiscal Year 2024-25.
