• This resolution allocates $4,300 to Chabad @ FSU for their Pegisha conference in
Crown Heights, New York. Pegisha is an annual global conference hosted by Chabad
on Campus International that brings together thousands of Jewish college students.
Pegisha offers workshops, lectures, networking, and immersive Shabbat programming
that foster leadership development, cultural exchange, and spiritual connection.
Participants will represent FSU on a global stage and return with new skills and
perspectives to strengthen Jewish life on campus, plan inclusive programs, and create
opportunities that engage and benefit the broader FSU community. This allocation will
cover the costs of airfare, ground transportation, hotel rooms, and registration fees for
twenty members of the organization.
• This resolution allocates $4,000.00 to Women in Business for their Harvard Women in
Business Intercollegiate Business Convention (IBC) in Boston, Massachusetts. IBC is
the world’s largest student-led business conference for women, bringing together nearly
1,000 participants to hear from keynote speakers, engage with industry professionals,
attend specialized panels, and network with top companies. Attending this conference
allows FSU students to represent the university on a national stage while developing
leadership skills, expanding professional networks, and gaining insight into industries
such as technology, finance, healthcare, entrepreneurship, and fashion. This allocation
will cover the costs of airfare, ground transportation, hotel rooms, and registration fees
for sixteen members of the organization. Funding was increased from $3,530.16 to
$4,000 on the senate floor. ‘Allocation after score’ represents committee decision and
therefore, will remain as $3,530.16.

Registered Student Organizations (RSOs) are integral to the cultural, educational, and social
fabric of the campus community. They play a critical role in promoting diversity, leadership
development, and student involvement. This funding will support these organizations inDocusign Envelope ID: E850FCA0-2BB2-465D-B606-A2C66B5985B1

Summary of Legislation:
This resolution proposes the allocation of $9,402.38 to various Registered Student
Organizations (RSOs) who requested funding from SGA’s RSO Allocation Committee. The
individual requests for each RSO are detailed below:
• PorColombia at FSU requests $1,188.23 to host the National President of
PorColombia for a campus address that promotes Colombian culture, leadership
development, and student engagement, fostering intercultural understanding
and professional growth for the FSU community. Request was amended to
$1,509.63 on senate floor.
• The Brazilian Student Association requests $1,750.00 to support member travel to the
BRASA Summit Americas 2025 in Boston, MA, providing professional development,
networking, and career opportunities while bringing back skills, resources, and global
engagement benefits to the broader FSU student body.
• The Society of Women Engineers requests $4,142.75 to attend the SWE National
Conference, enabling members to network with industry leaders, gain career
insights, and strengthen FSU’s representation in STEM while bringing back
professional connections and opportunities to the broader student body.
• The Society of Physics Students requests $2,000.00 to send members to the
Physics and Astronomy Congress, where they will present research, attend
workshops with Nobel laureates, and gain professional and academic insights to
bring back expanded knowledge, networking opportunities, and graduate school
preparation resources for the FSU student body.
• The Irresistible GarNettes requests $3,000 funding to host a performing arts event
that connects FSU students with aspiring youth performers, fostering
mentorship, collaboration, and community engagement while strengthening the
campus arts community and promoting Florida State to future students. They
were zero-funded.

Short Title: Approving funding recommendations from the RSO Allocation Committee
(RSOAC).
Summary of Legislation:
This resolution proposes the allocation of $6,084.00 to various Recognized Student
Organizations (RSOs) that requested funding from SGA’s RSO Allocation Committee. The
individual requests for each RSO are detailed below:
• This resolution allocates $5000.00 to SASA for their trip, which will amplify career
readiness and professional growth across FSU. Delegates will return with new skills,
insights, and employer connections to share through campus workshops, mock
interviews, and resume sessions. By enhancing FSU’s visibility with recruiters and
integrating leadership training into collaborative programming with other RSOs, the
impact will extend well beyond attendees—strengthening pipelines for internships, jobs,
and professional development opportunities for the entire student body.
• Chabad at FSU will host hundreds of students for the High Holidays, providing
traditional meals, services, and a welcoming space for Jewish students far from home.
These gatherings foster cultural understanding, inclusivity, and community by
welcoming peers of all backgrounds to join. The result is a meaningful celebration that
strengthens Jewish identity while enriching the broader FSU student experience through
dialogue, respect, and shared tradition. They were zero funded.
• This resolution allocates $1084.00 to FSU students that will compete in a fast-paced
international case competition hosted at one of Canada’s leading business institutions,
solving two cases in just one week. This experience sharpens problem-solving,
teamwork, and presentation skills while connecting students with global peers and
professionals. Delegates will bring back insights to share through campus workshops
and networking events, enhancing career readiness and professional opportunities for
the broader FSU community.Docusign Envelope ID: B01255ED-8CA7-4204-BE58-A6E577CFFABD

Summary of Legislation:
This resolution proposes the allocation of $12,982.16 to various RSOs who request funding
from the RSOAC:
• Request #1 - Relay For Life - $3,198.16
o Context: Relay for Life is a non-profit organization dedicated to providing and
supporting the battle against cancer. Being a non-profit organization means they
are ineligible to use fundraising in any other manner than for the purpose of
cancer research. Thus, SGA is the primary source of funding for programming.
With an event that will host over 100 different organizations, the committee voted
in favor of waiving the maximum amount of $3,000 and recommending $3,198.16
unanimously.
• Request #2 - Phi Alpha Delta Pre-Law Fraternity - $0
o Context: While requesting money for airfare to travel to Washington D.C. to
compete in the Phi Alpha Delta national law case competition. An event our local
chapter was fortunate enough to come in second place last year and took home
the most awards out of any chapter with nine. The biggest obstacle for the
committee was the fact twenty students were selected to attend and the original
request was $6,000.00. Ultimately, the organization did admit they had done a
fair amount of fundraising and were comfortable covering the cost regardless of
the funding amount, and they had gone on the trip last year under a similar figure
without SGA’s funding. Thus, the committee opted to fund over half the original
amount. Zero-funded on senate floor.
• Request #3 - Classical Guitar Society - $2,900.00Docusign Envelope ID: 0F88399C-6A5D-4C10-806E-F6FDBFB5F817

sections.heading: Page 2
sections.text:
o Context: In a contract funding request, the Classical Guitar Society will be
bringing three acclaimed and influential classical guitarists to perform over the
course of three days. In an effort to ensure the growth of FSU’s arts and cultures,
the committee voted to fund the original request for $2,900.
o The event will have a minimum of 175 students in attendance and is open to the
public to attend.
• Request #4 - Students For The Exploration And Development Of Space at FAMU
and FSU - $4,800.00
o Context: This organization had originally $5,000 for a total of 16 students to
attend a prestigious space networking event being held in Seattle. They have
taken exceptional steps to fundraise; originally, the cost per student would have
been over $600 each. Without our help, their fundraising efforts have already
reduced the cost to $400 per person. With this additional funding, each student
will only pay $125. Allowing them to perform on the highest level in the
aerospace industry, and bring their connections back to not only FSU, but FAMU
as well.
• Request #5 – Business Case Club - $668.00
o Context: The Business Case Club will be taking four students to represent our
school on the highest levels, one such at Georgetown University to compete
against even Ivy League Schools. Opening the door to our university to host
speakers, networking events, and even a competition of our own in the future.
• Request #6 – Business Case Club - $1,416.00
o Context: The Business Case Club will be taking four students to represent our
school on the highest levels, one such at London, Ontario, Canada to compete
Internationally. Opening the door to our university to host speakers, networking
events, and even a competition of our own in the future. The committee valued
this opportunity and voted to waive the maximum amount to facilitate this event.

• Big Sister Little Sister was allocated $4,970.00 for a community service trip to New
Orleans, LA. The trip will benefit the wider student body by enabling participants to
acquire and subsequently share valuable leadership, teamwork, and community
engagement skills through presentations and events. The initiative is also critical for
strengthening the organization's reputation, boosting recruitment appeal, and inspiring
peers to get involved by visibly showcasing the value of service and leadership
development.
• Every Nation Campus (ENC) was allocated $4,975.00 for its annual ENC North America
conference trip. This trip allows FSU students to represent the university, showcase
their character and strength, and solidify ENC Tallahassee's national reputation. Their
presence has been impactful, notably by performing the War Chant and leading to
students choosing FSU because of the community they saw. ENC Tallahassee has also
been recognized for its service to college students and has been asked to plan and
execute the "Wild N Out" session for the second consecutive year, offering FSU
students a unique opportunity for fun and cross-campus engagement. The organization
has received funding for this conference for the past four years.
• The Big Event Tallahassee was allocated $4,959.32 for its service initiatives. The Big
Event Tallahassee is a beloved service tradition for students from FSU, TSC, and
FAMU, dedicated to giving back to the Tallahassee community. Recognizing the
support from local residents, businesses, and non-profits, the organization hosts two
annual service projects: The Little Event (Fall) and The Big Event (Spring). Following a
decline in participation since the pandemic, the organization is committed to restoring
The Big Event to its former size and maximizing its community impact. Recent efforts
show promising results, with The Little Event on September 27th attracting over 500
volunteers (double the previous year). The organization's goal is to recruit over 1,500Docusign Envelope ID: 1B25993D-14AD-4CA7-A6F8-02F392C39986

that this allocation will help surpass that goal.
• STITCH was allocated $356.00 for its programming and events. STITCH focuses on
providing students with a space for artistic expression, creative showcase, and the
acquisition of practical skills like sewing. Students gain valuable resume experience in
garment creation, editorial work, photoshoots, and fashion design, fostering creative
and leadership growth. The allocated funds will help bridge the financial gap required to
execute high-quality events, particularly their main focus: the end-of-year, student-run
fashion runway show. Expenses include materials for set design, sewing supplies for
workshops, and venue rentals to create fully realized production stages. Though the
organization actively fundraises through methods like Share-It Nights and Market
Wednesday garage sales, they require this assistance to ensure the continued success
of their creative programming.
• The Filipino Student Association (FSA) was allocated $1,953.48 for its annual Parol Ball
banquet. The Parol Ball has significant learning value, promoting diversity awareness
through authentic Filipino food, cultural decorations, and performances by the cultural
dance team, "Indak." It serves to foster a strong sense of community and inclusivity on
campus, fulfilling FSA's mission to increase awareness of Filipino culture by uniting
diverse students in a shared celebration.
• The South Asian Student Association was allocated $2,266.15 for its annual Diwali
Banquet. The annual Diwali Banquet is a critical event that celebrates one of the most
important festivals in South Asian culture, offering a unique opportunity for the entire
FSU community to experience traditions rooted in the values of light, unity, and hope.
Given the smaller South Asian population on campus, this banquet provides a crucial
sense of belonging for South Asian students while allowing the wider FSU student body
to engage in meaningful cross-cultural celebration. The requested funds will ensure the
event remains a vibrant and memorable experience, featuring free food and high-quality
cultural performances that embody the joyous, communal spirit of Diwali.

Allocation Resolution #: 77-009
Primary Sponsor(s): Goldstein

Short Title: Approving funding recommendations from the College Leadership Council (CLC)
Funding Committee
Summary of Legislation: This resolution proposes the allocation of $20,000 to various
College Leadership Councils (CLCs) as recommended by the College Leadership Council
Funding Committee. These allocations will support programming, outreach, and professional
development initiatives within each college, promoting academic and leadership engagement
among Florida State University students.
The CLC Funding Committee met during the Fall 2025 semester to review and deliberate on
funding requests submitted by each College Leadership Council in accordance with Chapter
622 of the Student Body Statutes. Following review hearings and discussion, the Committee
approved the attached allocations for the 2025-2026 Fiscal Year.
Background Information:
College Leadership Councils (CLCs) serve as the official representative and leadership bodies
for students within their respective academic colleges. Functioning as entities of the Executive
Branch, each Council works closely with its college administration to promote academic
success, leadership development, and student engagement. The CLC Funding Committee,
composed of two students appointed by the Student Body President, two student Senators
appointed by the Student Senate President, and chaired by the Student Body Treasurer, was
established to equitably distribute a block of funds designated by the Student Senate Budget
Committee each fiscal year. This structure ensures transparent, accountable allocation of
funds to support initiatives that strengthen the academic and professional experiences of FSU
students within their respective colleges.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
Upon approval by the Student Senate, the allocated funds will be transferred to the
corresponding College Leadership Councils for use in the 2025-2026 Fiscal Year. Councils will
use these funds to host academic and professional development events, community
engagement programs, and leadership initiatives consistent with the goals of their colleges and
Student Government Association policy. The passage of this resolution affirms the Senate’s
continued support of the College Leadership Council program and reinforces SGA’sDocusign Envelope ID: 6A1CCDAA-8561-4A9B-971F-DE3AAD05940F

77th STUDENT SENATE
Legislation Cover Sheet
Allocation Resolution #: 010
Primary Sponsor(s): Nucatola, Rios
Co-sponsor(s): Berg, Collantes
Short Title: Approving funding recommendations from the RSO Allocation Committee
(RSOAC).
Summary of Legislation:
This resolution proposes the allocation of $4,635.47 to various Registered Student
Organizations (RSOs) who requested funding from SGA’s RSO Allocation Committee. The
individual requests for each RSO are detailed below:
• The Association for Computing Machinery received $635.47 for their ACM’S Fall
2025 Programming Contest hosted on 11/22/25. This event is offered every
semester to all students that want to participate. The programming contest is a day
of coding in a team, a valuable skill in the workforce. Expecting everyone to walk
away having experienced working in a team and practicing their programming
skills. The learning value is that they practice skills learned in CS (and related)
coursework, but being a CS student is not required. Professors have historically
given extra credit to students who participate in the contest, which shows that our
professors support the semesterly event.
• The Diverse World Fashion Magazine received $4,000 for their magazine printing
costs for their events. Diverse World Fashion Magazine exists to celebrate the
incredible diversity of our student body and show how different cultures express
themselves through fashion and style. Each semester, our completely student-run
magazine highlights creativity, inclusivity, and the unique perspectives that make
our campus so vibrant. They distribute free magazines to all FSU students during
Market Wednesday and our Magazine Release Events
• The Undergraduate Law Review was $0 funded due to constraints of the amount of
people they are taking on the trip.
Background Information:
Registered Student Organizations (RSOs) are integral to the cultural, educational, and social
fabric of the campus community. They play a critical role in promoting diversity, leadership
development, and student involvement. This funding will support these organizations in
carrying out impactful programming or travel that aligns with FSU's values of community
building, professional development, and discovery.Docusign Envelope ID: 4521E2FA-449D-4589-801F-4DDB33A79DD2

sections.heading: Page 2
sections.text:
The RSO Allocation Committee was created as a means for RSOs to obtain SGA funding for
programming and travel needs. All events and travel opportunities funded must be available
and/or beneficial to all members of the Student Body.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
Following approval by the Student Senate, funds will be transferred to the RSO for the stated
purpose in the resolution. They will be required to submit receipts and an event evaluation
form to the SGA Accounting Office within ten (10) business days of the event or travel. The
financial support provided will empower the RSOs to carry out impactful activities to drive
cultural engagement and professional growth.

• Attachment #1: Authorizing Resolution
• Attachment #2: Proposed Transfer Excel Sheet
• Attachment #3: Grading Rubrics and attendance sheetDocusign Envelope ID: 4521E2FA-449D-4589-801F-4DDB33A79DD2

Short Title: Proclamation honoring the late President Jimmy Carter (39th U.S. President)
Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation aims to summarize the accomplishments made by President Jimmy Carter
during his presidency and the immense service he continued to give along with his wife, the
late Mrs. Rosalynn Carter. Since President Carter died on December 29, 2024 it is important
for the Student Senate to illuminate his positive impact on America and the world.
Background Information:
Recently, President Carter died on December 29, 2024. President Jimmy Carter left a lasting
impact through his presidency, during which he championed diversity, social justice,
environmental preservation, education, and equity through his acts as the 39th President. After
losing the opportunity to be reelected upon President Reagan’s win in the 1980 presidential
election, President Carter continued to use his influence to strengthen democracy and just
governments in countries found in regions such as Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East.
By establishing the Carter Center and the Carter Work project (a program within the
organization Habitat for Humanity), President Jimmy Carter and First Lady Rosalynn Carter
continued to be servant leaders long after residing in the White House. Through examining
President Carter’s life events, student leaders can view an optimal example of a selfless,
patriotic leader.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
If enacted by the 77th Student Senate, this proclamation would echo the values of Vires, Artes,
and Mores. President Jimmy Carter exemplified strength in his values, skillful leadership, and
virtuous character throughout his life. It is intended a formalized copy of this letter be sent to
the Carter Center.

Proclamation #: 004
Primary Sponsor(s): Rodriguez
Co-sponsor(s): Mendez-Arango, Murphy, Pierre-Mendoza, Rios, Salazar-Angeles
Short Title: This proclamation condemns the measures of Florida SB 2-C, which overlook
students in the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program who reside in Florida
by unfairly revoking them of in-state tuition.
Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation addresses the recent passage of SB 2-C into Florida law and its mandatory
measures that demand undocumented students pay out-of-state tuition in Florida post-
secondary education institutions. This action blankets over students under the Deferred Action
for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, otherwise known as “Dreamers,” in Florida, despite
them being brought to this country under circumstances beyond their control when they were
very young, along with growing up in Florida and having attended secondary school and high
school in Florida. Furthermore, this proclamation shows our Senate’s disapproval of our
legislature’s actions and urges that our university acknowledges this unfounded discriminatory
anti-immigration bill and provides resources to Dreamers that reside in our university to ease
the monetary and stigmatizing burden SB 2-C will evoke come July 1, 2025.
Background Information:
On February 13, 2025, SB 2-C and other anti-immigration bills were signed into law by
Governor Ron Desantis after being passed through Florida’s legislature. This bill includes
measures that revoke in-state tuition from undocumented students who reside in Florida.
However, under these terms, students within the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals
(DACA) program are included due to them being considered as “undocumented immigrants.”
This bill includes them despite most having grown up in the states, having completed their
secondary education in Florida, and being required to complete their high school education to
even be eligible for DACA.
In June of 2012, the DACA program was established by the Obama Administration to ensure
the protection of children who were brought to the U.S when they were young from removal
processes and enabling them work authorization. DACA was brought in order to protect youths
who were brought into this country under circumstances beyond their control and support them
accordingly.Docusign Envelope ID: 745CD4E8-D93A-4BAD-93E5-26F03346EB18

sections.heading: Page 2
sections.text:
In 2014, HB 851 was signed into law by former Governor Rick Scott that allowed Dreamers to
pay in-state tuition rates in post-secondary education institutions within Florida if they met
certain criterion under F.S 1009.26. This is now dismissed under SB 2-C, denying Dreamers of
in-state tuition and forcing them along with other “undocumented” students to pay out-of-state
tuition starting July 1, 2025.
This bill pressures Dreamers with an outstanding economic burden, along with further
stigmatizing them and their legal status despite previous protections being installed within the
U.S and Florida state government that show empathy and discretion to their situation. Due to
the lack of permanency of DACA, as it was temporary solution to resolve struggles of
Dreamers, it is seen nationally how state legislatures are choosing to strip Dreamers of their
liberties and resources to pursue their aspirations that they rightfully deserve and have earned.
Florida is following suit, as this bill dehumanizes Dreamers, overlooking the countless
distributions to their country they provide through economic means, as Dreamers and eligible
DACA individuals have provided roughly $304 million in federal and state taxes in 2021
according to the American Immigration Council.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
The university and student senate will acknowledge how SB 2-C targets it’s students under
DACA and the university will take onto itself the action of seeking and providing Dreamers with
resources to help them continue their post-secondary education in Florida State University.

Short Title: Support of LGBTQ+ Housing at Florida State University
Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation provides formal support for an LGBTQ+ housing option on the FSU Housing
Portal to ensure all students have access to safe residential spaces. It also acknowledges the
collaboration between the student body, the Student Government Association, and the
university administration to reinstate the LGBTQ+ housing option.
Background Information:
Senator Murphy began drafting this proclamation after meeting with the president of the Pride
Student Union, the largest campus organization for the LGBTQ+ community. The Pride
Student Union was concerned with the recent removal of the LGBTQ+ housing option on the
FSU Housing Portal. An LGBTQ+ housing option gives this community a safe living
environment. The Pride Student Union and the Inter-Residence Hall Council each released
public statements in support of the LGBTQ+ housing option.
Senator Murphy and a representative from the Pride Student Union each met with the head of
FSU Housing to fully understand the situation. As of Wednesday, February 12th, 2025, FSU
Housing reinstated the LGBTQ+ Housing Option.
This proclamation acknowledges the work and collaboration among the university
administration, student government, and various campus organizations to reinstate the
LGBTQ+ housing option. The LGBTQ+ housing ensures all students at FSU will be safe and
welcomed.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
This legislation would declare a formal opinion of the 77th Student Senate: expressing support
for an LGBTQ+ housing option on the FSU Housing Portal. In expressing this opinion, the 77th
Student Senate will promote a safer and more inclusive environment for the student body. It is
vital that the voice of the student body—the student senate—is heard on this matter to protect
marginalized communities in the future. This proclamation also promotes future collaboration
between the student body, Student Government Association, and university administration by
acknowledging the collaboration done to reinstate the LGBTQ+ housing option.

Short Title: Proclamation honoring the late State Senator Geraldine Thompson
Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation recognizes the impactful contributions of State Senator Geraldine
Thompson to Florida’s political and social landscape. Her dedication to public service,
education, and civil rights left an enduring legacy. Her tireless advocacy for marginalized
communities and commitment to justice and equality have shaped the lives of many Floridians
and specifies the voting thresholds required for passage of each type of legislation.
Background Information:
State Senator Geraldine Thompson dedicated her career to advancing civil rights, improving
educational opportunities, and championing social justice. A trailblazer in Florida politics, she
was the first African American woman elected to represent District 12 in the Florida House of
Representatives. Senator Thompson was instrumental in preserving African American history
through her efforts with the Wells’ Built Museum of African American History and Culture. Her
passion for equity and education reform made her a respected leader across party lines. Her
passing marks the loss of a true champion for justice, equity, and the betterment of her
community.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
If enacted by the Student Senate, this proclamation would honor the values of leadership,
integrity, and dedication exemplified by Senator Thompson. It would acknowledge her
contributions to the state of Florida and serve as an inspiration for future leaders to continue
her legacy of service and advocacy.

Short Title: Proclamation on TPS Designation for Venezuelans
Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation gives context as to the situation that Venezuelans are facing, including
students, who are under TPS (Temporary Protected Status) currently. The removal of this
status is explained, specifically the detrimental effects that this will have on students who are
trying to complete their education at higher institutions like Florida State University.
Background Information:
This is important to bring up to Senate, as a significant percentage of the Hispanic population
on campus is Venezuelan and some are under TPS and may be unable to finish their studies
after the status expires. This protected status has been in effect since 2021 and currently there
are no other pathways for Venezuelans to stay in the United States legally, therefore they
would be at risk for deportation if they wished to stay and complete their studies or work that
they have already started.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
This is just a way of making the percentage of the student body that this is referring to know
that we are here to support them in this tumultuous time, especially as a lot of issues with
immigration are uncertain and on pause.

A PROCLAMATION

WHEREAS, The population of Hispanic/Latino students on Florida State’s Campus makes up almost a1
quarter of the student population, with a large percentage of them from Venezuela and some living2
in the United States under Temporary Protected Status (TPS); and3
WHEREAS, The Venezuela TPS Act of 2019 was created with the intention of making a legal pathway4
for Venezuelans to escape the dangerous and hostile political environment within the country of5
Venezuela; and; and6
WHEREAS, After the Act was introduced in the Senate in 2019, it was finally passed in March of 2021,7
furthermore granting TPS status to Venezuelan migrants living in the United States ; and8
WHEREAS, There were two TPS designations made, one in 2021 and another in 2023. The latter 20239
designation was extended for 18 months on January 17th, 2025 by Secretary of Homeland10
Security, Alejandro Mayorkas, which would have extended this aforementioned status until October11
2nd, 2026; and12
WHEREAS, During this extension period, Venezuelans would have been granted the time to find13
pathways to residency and citizenship without being in danger in their own country; and;14
WHEREAS, This extension was vacated on January 28th, 2025 by the newly instated Secretary of15
Homeland Security, Kristi Noem, meaning that the status of 2023 applicants would be terminated16
on April 7th, 2025, halting all legal status for Venezuelans, who would have had another year and a17
half to secure another legal status to stay in the Unites States; and18
WHEREAS, This means that Venezuelans, including students, who fall under Temporary Protected19
Status, regardless of the year they applied and the span of time they’ve been in the country, will be20
able to be deported after April 7th, 2025 (2023 designation) and September 10th, 2025 (202121
designation); and22Docusign Envelope ID: FB2EE55A-6829-42BB-B987-00F09B5DADC2

Short Title: Reaffirming Florida State’s Student Senate support for the role of identity-based
agencies on campus
Summary of Legislation:
This resolution aims to reaffirm the Student Senate’s support for the role of identity-based
agencies on campus. This is important in light of recent acts targeting members within these
communities.
Background Information:
The first student agency established at Florida State University was the Black Student Union
in 1968. As of 2025, Florida State has seven identity agencies established to provide support,
advocacy and community for students within those identities at the university. Each agency
houses numerous RSOs within them that provide further support and inclusion. With that, as of
this year there have been multiple acts targeting members within these communities creating a
sense of tension within these communities. This has prompted multiple agencies at FSU to
release statements addressing these issues. Since one of the main goals of Student
Government is to represent and support all students on campus, this proclamation has been
created to reaffirm the student senate’s support and the role of identity-based organizations on
campus.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
The main effect of this legislation is to show the Senate’s support of agencies to the student
body and other interested individuals. By doing this, the Student Senate will show its support
for the role and purpose of identity-based organizations.

diversity efforts, and strengthened the university's national standing. This proclamation is being
written to honor his legacy following his passing and to formally recognize his profound impact
on the FSU community.

of President John E. Thrasher by the Florida State University Student Senate. It would enter an
official statement of tribute into the Senate record and direct that a copy of the proclamation be
shared with President Thrasher’s family. While symbolic in nature, it serves as the Student
Body's formal expression of gratitude and remembrance.

Short Title: Increasing Accessibility of the Seminole Express
Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation aims to encourage the installation of additional seating, benches, and
shelters that are provided at Seminole Express bus stops on- and off-campus. It explains why
investing in this project would be beneficial to the student body, the University, and members
of FSU’s community. It also provides suggestions and recommendations for planning to
implement these changes.
Background Information:
Since parking availability is a challenging issue across campus, it is in the University’s best
interests to invest time and effort into increasing the accessibility of the Seminole Express. If a
greater percentage of our constituents feel that our public bus system is safe, comfortable, and
easy to use, then over time, there will be fewer people who opt to drive their cars to, from, and
around campus, and students may be less likely to bring their cars to Tallahassee with them if
they believe that they can rely on the buses. Promoting students to commute to campus
through the Seminole Express rather than utilizing private transportation would aid in reducing
congestion within parking garages. FSU is a walkable campus, but it’s not realistic to expect
everyone to be able to walk from one corner to another if they need to. We already have plenty
of bus stops around the campus loop that significantly cut down on the time it takes to get
from, for example, Diffenbaugh to Doak Campbell Stadium. To reach this goal, we need to
prioritize breaking down barriers that inhibit or discourage ridership by making the stops
themselves more universally accessible.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
This proclamation aims to increase awareness of the need for increased accessibility of the
Seminole Express, and offers potential solutions for how the university can work to achieve
this goal.

Short Title: Recognizing the Need for Kosher Food Accessibility at Florida State University.
Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation recognizes the lack of kosher-certified dining options at Florida State
University and affirms the Student Senate’s commitment to equitable access to religiously
inclusive meals. It urges FSU administration and Seminole Dining to take steps toward
providing kosher food options in dining halls, retail locations, or designated meal plans.
Background Information:
Florida State University students who observe kosher dietary practices currently lack access to
certified kosher dining options on campus. Unlike vegan, vegetarian, and allergy-sensitive
options already available, kosher food is not offered in dining halls or retail locations. This
forces students who keep kosher to either seek costly alternatives off campus, restrict
participation in community dining, or go without meals altogether. Other universities across the
nation—including University of Florida, University of Maryland, and New York University—have
successfully incorporated kosher dining options, demonstrating both feasibility and student
demand. Addressing this gap at FSU is an important step toward fostering religious inclusivity
and supporting the wellbeing of Jewish students.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
If enacted, this proclamation would formally establish the Student Senate’s recognition of the
absence of kosher dining on campus as a barrier to inclusivity. It would also record the
Senate’s official support for expanding dining services to include kosher-certified options,
signaling student advocacy for this issue to FSU administration and campus dining partners.

Short Title: Recognizing Indigenous Peoples’ Day
Summary of Legislation:
The proclamation recognizes Indigenous Peoples’ Day as a day honoring the histories,
cultures, and perspectives of Native Americans and Indigenous peoples. It encourages Florida
State University to continue to work with the Seminole Tribe of Florida and other Native
American and Indigenous partners to create a mutually beneficial future through continuing to
foster collaborative scholarship and cultural development.
Background Information:
Since 1912, members of the Native American and Indigenous communities have sought a day
recognizing the culture and contributions of their peoples. Since then, 17 states and
Washington DC have established state holidays honoring Native Americans and Indigenous
peoples, and many municipalities, including many in Florida, have proclaimed a similar day of
commemoration. The Florida Senate, pursuant to HR 8087, declared Monday, October 13, as
Indigenous Peoples’ Day. As Florida State University actively recognizes its campuses are
located on Native American and Indigenous lands and seeks to promote friendship and
advancement of these peoples, recognition of a day honoring Native American and Indigenous
peoples is an important step in pursuing these goals.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
If enacted, this proclamation would formally establish the Student Senate’s recognition of
Indigenous Peoples’ Day as a day honoring the history, cultures, and perspectives of Native
American and Indigenous peoples. It would also reaffirm the Senate’s official support for the
continued strength of FSU’s relationship with the Seminole Tribe of Florida and mission to
work with the Seminole Tribe of Florida and other Native American and Indigenous partners to
continue fostering cultural education, scholarship, and growth.

Short Title: Recognizing October as National Breast Cancer Awareness Month
Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation formally recognizes October as National Breast Cancer Awareness Month
(NBCAM) and brings attention to all those impacted within the Florida State University
community by breast cancer. It presents relevant research and history on the issue,
emphasizes the importance of early detection, and highlights work already being done within
the university to combat breast cancer.
Background Information:
NBCAM, founded in 1985 through the American Cancer Society, Imperial Chemical Industries,
and First Lady Betty Ford, aims to promote education, early detection, and research. This
legislation recognizes FSU’s contributions to that mission through the work of researchers
such as Dr. Qing-Xiang “Amy” Sang and Professor Bonnie Spring. It also highlights student
journalist Holden Grace Wilkins, who brought visibility to this research. By adopting this
proclamation, the Student Senate honors the survivors, advocates, and scholars within the
FSU community who advance awareness and inspire hope.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
If passed, this proclamation would recognize and bring further attention to National Breast
Cancer Awareness Month, while positively recognizing members of our campus community
who have been putting in the work to combat this issue through research and advocacy.

campaign, as she was herself was diagnosed and survived breast cancer when her husband,4
Gerald Ford, was president of the United States, which brought increased awareness of the topic to5

WHEREAS, Breast cancer is the second most common cancer among women in the United States7
according to the Center for Disease Prevention and Control, and roughly one in eight women will be8
diagnosed with breast cancer within their lifetime, showcasing how important and necessary9
preventative treatment and early detection is; and10
WHEREAS, Breast cancer is widely recognized as a women’s health issue, but it is essential to11
acknowledge that men are also impacted, with approximately 1 in 726 men diagnosed and an12
estimated 510 losing their lives to the disease in their lifetime, highlighting the importance of13
inclusive education and awareness for all; and14

and communities, as its emotional, physical, and financial impacts extend far beyond the individual,16
with the American Cancer Society estimating over 310,000 new cases in the United States in 2025,17
reminding us that awareness, early detection, and continued research are vital to save lives and18

Short Title: Support for the 2025 Tech Fee Project Request from the Department of Student

Summary of Legislation:
This resolution expresses the Florida State University Student Senate’s support for the 2025
Technology Fee proposal submitted by the Office of Student Governance & Advocacy to
enhance the audio-visual system in the Student Senate Chambers. The project includes new
ceiling-array microphones, broadcast cameras, a presenter-facing monitor, and an A/V control
system to improve accessibility, transparency, and hybrid participation for Student Government
meetings.
Background Information:
The Student Senate Chambers serve as the official meeting space for the 80-member Student
Senate, the Congress of Graduate Students, and other SGA entities. The current A/V setup is
outdated and limits accessibility, hybrid engagement, and broadcast quality. The Department
of Student Engagement and the Office of Student Governance & Advocacy have submitted a
2025 Technology Fee proposal requesting funding for modernized A/V infrastructure. The
proposal has received endorsement from Dr. Zduy Chu, Associate Vice President for Student
Affairs, for aligning with FSU’s Strategic Plan priorities of transparency, accessibility, and
student engagement.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
If adopted, this resolution will formally record the Student Senate’s support for the Technology
Fee proposal and encourage the University’s Technology Fee Advisory Committee and
Information Technology Services to fund and implement the project. The resolution does not
allocate Student Government funds and carries no fiscal impact to the Senate budget.

Dear Dr. Fozard:
I am pleased to offer my strong support for an upcoming project within the Student Governance & Advocacy
office to enhance the audio-visual capabilities of the Student Senate Chambers in the Student Union. This
proposal seeks Student Technology Fee funding to install ceiling-array microphones, additional broadcast
cameras, a rear-facing video monitor, and a dedicated A/V control station. These upgrades will significantly
improve the transparency and accessibility of Student Government Association (SGA) proceedings, directly
benefiting all of the nearly 42,000 students represented by SGA on the main campus.
The proposed improvements will allow meetings of the Student Senate, Congress of Graduate Students, SGA
committees, and other student groups and campus partners to be livestreamed and recorded with
professional quality. This project will also improve accessibility for students participating in these events in
person by ensuring clear, room-wide audio pickup and by supporting hybrid participation. In addition, the
upgraded A/V system will benefit other campus stakeholders who use the Senate Chambers throughout the
year for guest speakers, alumni events, and special forums.
As you know, the Student Technology Fee provides critical support to projects that advance instructional
technology across the University. This project is closely aligned with the statutorily allowed uses of the Fee
and will advance key initiatives in FSU’s Strategic Plan, including promoting engaged learning, supporting
student success, and fostering innovation and excellence in campus resources. Unlike academic colleges and
central IT organizations, the Division of Student Affairs (which includes the Student Governance & Advocacy
office) does not receive an annual direct allocation of Student Technology Fee funds and therefore relies on
the competitive Student Technology Fee allocation process to advance critical student-facing technology
projects.
Thank you for your consideration of this proposal. We welcome the opportunity to discuss this project further
with you and the Student Technology Fee Advisory Committee. In the meantime, please feel free to contact
Andy Johnson, Program Director for Student Governance & Advocacy, at ajohnson23@fsu.edu or (850) 645-
0908 with any questions or for additional information.
Best regards,
Zduy Chu, Ed.D.

77th STUDENT SENATE
Legislation Cover Sheet
Senate Proclamation #: 26
Primary Sponsor(s): Druckmann, Cordero
Short Title: Supports sexual assault awareness and prevention practice and recognition at
Florida State University.
Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation serves in efforts to create a safe, respectful, and supportive campus
environment. It acknowledges the prevalence of sexual violence on college campuses and
encourages FSU's dedication to prevention, education, and express support for all survivors.
Background Information:
This proclamation arises from the present public health crisis of sexual violence on college
campuses; a problem the university community acknowledges and has an existing
commitment to address. The legislative background highlights alarming statistics, including
that 1 in 5 women and 1 in 16 men are sexually assaulted while in college, and that nearly a
third of sexually victimized students drop out of school entirely, according to RAINN.
Furthermore, a lack of awareness about available support is noted, with less than half of
students at the University of Florida knowing about their campus's sexual misconduct
resources. While Florida State University already provides resources like the RSO Students for
Sexual Assault Awareness (SSAA) and the kNOw MORE initiative, the Student Senate is
calling for an enhanced, active response with more protective measures to ensure a safer and
more supportive environment.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
The effect of this legislation is to formalize the Student Senate's position by officially urging
Florida State University to enhance its protective measures and resource availability against
sexual violence. It specifically mandates an increase in advocacy and awareness for existing
support services, while also recommending the adaptation of new practices, such as providing
and advertising self-defense tools and classes to increase campus and individual safety for all
students.

19 measures to increase campus and individual safety. With the above resources present on campus,

21 new practices providing self-defense tools and classes advertised to all students

Senate Proclamation #: 417
Primary Sponsor(s): Goldstein, LoBianco
Co-sponsor(s): All Senators
Short Title: A Proclamation Honoring the Victims and Community Response to the April 17,
2025, Tragedy at Florida State University
Summary of Legislation:
This proclamation, issued by the Student Senate President and the Student Senate President
Pro Tempore on behalf of the 77th Student Senate and the Student Government Association,
commemorates the lives lost and the individuals injured during the April 17, 2025, active
shooter incident at Florida State University. It recognizes the profound grief and trauma
experienced by the campus community, honors the extraordinary efforts of first responders
and university personnel, and establishes April 17th as the "FSU Day of Reflection and
Resilience" in remembrance and unity.
Background Information:
On April 17, 2025, a shooting took place inside the FSU Student Union, resulting in the deaths
of two beloved community members: Robert Morales and Tiru Chabba, and injuries to six
others. Countless students, staff, and faculty were forced to shelter in place, unsure if they
would be safe. The incident deeply affected thousands of members of the university family and
has left a lasting impact on the emotional, academic, and professional lives of many.
The FSU community responded with overwhelming courage, compassion, and unity. Vigils
were held. Class policies were adapted. Support centers were opened. And students, faculty,
and staff alike found ways to hold one another through a time of profound difficulty.
Effect of Proposed Legislation:
If proclaimed, this resolution becomes the official statement of the Student Government
Association and serves as a lasting tribute to those lost, a formal acknowledgment of those
injured and traumatized, and a commitment to remembering April 17th each year as a day of
resilience and shared reflection.

Chapter 1113 Civic Engagement Board Garnet & Gold Voting Commission
1113.1 Purpose and Creation
The Civic Engagement Board (CEB) shall be an affiliated project of the
Student Government Association designed to engage and educate the
campus community in the critical institutions within our local, state, and
national political systems.
1113.2 Executive Board
A. Executive Director
The Executive Director of the Civic Engagement Board shall
have the following privileges, responsibilities and duties:
1. Serve as the primary external affairs officer and point of
contact for the CEB.
2. Provide regular updates to the Student Senate.
3. Collaborate with the Executive Branch and other SGA
entities as necessary.
4. Develops goals that guide board activities.
5. Guides priorities of the board and ensures goals are
being met by regularly advising and supervising
assistant directors in their work and providing aid when
necessary.
6. Focuses on developing institutional changes to improve
civic engagement at a foundational level.
7. Be financially certified.
8. Be appointed by the Student Body President and
confirmed by the Student Senate in accordance with
Chapter 304.
B. Deputy Director
The Deputy Director of the Civic Engagement Board shall have
the following privileges, responsibilities and duties:
1. Manage and supervise Director-level positions.
2. Serve as the Chair of the Garnet & Gold Voting
Commission.
3. Assist the Executive Director in their duties.DocuSign Envelope ID: 7AF0EFC4-96FC-40D7-B115-53B021D350E6

sections.text:
4. Serve as acting-Executive Director in the Executive
Director’s absence.
5. Be appointed by the Student Body President and
confirmed by the Student Senate in accordance with
Chapter 304.
C. Director of Finance
The Director of Finance of the Civic Engagement Board shall
have the following privileges, responsibilities and duties:
1. Serve as the chief financial officer of the CEB, and
perform all duties necessary in the management of
finances.
2. Collaborate with University faculty and staff for grant
funding.
3. Be financially certified.
4. Be appointed by the Student Body President and
confirmed by the Student Senate in accordance with
Chapter 304.
D. Director of Communications
The Director of Communications of the Civic Engagement
Board shall have the following privileges, responsibilities and
duties:
1. Coordinate information distribution across campus.
2. Coordinate with Leon County Supervisor of Elections
office to receive and distribute voter information.
3. Run CEB social media accounts.
E. Director of Programming
The Director of Programming of the Civic Engagement Board
shall have the following privileges, responsibilities and duties:
1. Develops programming on behalf of the CEB and the
Garnet & Gold Voting Commission.
2. Coordinate with relevant on-campus entities to increase
collaboration and outreach in programming.
3. Coordinate with the Director of Finance to ensure the
proper allocation of funds for events.

The Director of Research of the Civic Engagement Board shallDocuSign Envelope ID: 7AF0EFC4-96FC-40D7-B115-53B021D350E6

1113.3 Selection and Term of Office
A. In the event of a vacancy of an Executive Board position,
applications shall open and shall be have an individual selected
to fill the vacancy within one month of the application opening.

ought to be taken into consideration in the selection of these

with assistance from the Deputy Director.
E. In the event of a resignation, the resigning individual shall turn
their resignation into the Executive Director. If the Executive
Director resigns, they shall turn their resignation into the
Student Body President.
1113.4 Garnet & Gold Voting Commission
A. During the Fall semester of a Midterm or General Election, the
CEB shall form the Garnet & Gold Voting Commission, which
shall engage key stakeholders to strategically increase civic
engagement and voter turnout among the FSU Student Body for
each election year through programming, education, and action.

Directors responsible for the operation of the Commission. The
Board of Directors shall be composed of the following members:
1. A designee of the SGA Executive Branch;

C. Prior to the Fall semester in which the Garnet & Gold Voting
Commission shall be formed, the Executive Director of the CEB
shall call a meeting with the Student Body President, Student
Senate President, and the SGA Advisor, in which they shall
decide any Registered Student Organizations or Campus
Entities that shall have a designee on the Commission.
D. The Deputy Director of the CEB shall serve as the Chair of the
Garnet & Gold Voting Commission
E. The Board of Directors shall meet no less than once every two
weeks between the appointment of all designees and the end of
the relevant election. These meetings shall be open to the
public and subject to all requirements of SGA meetings. The
Chair shall schedule these meetings, with consent of the Board
of Directors.
F. Following the end of the election, the Garnet & Gold Voting
Commission shall present a report of voter turnout and civic
engagement to the Student Senate.
1113.1 Purpose and Creation
The Garnet & Gold Voting Commission shall be an affiliated project of
the Student Government Association that shall occur every other year,
aligning with any school year that is an election year. The Garnet &
Gold Voting Commission shall engage key stakeholders to strategically
increase civic engagement and voter turnout among the FSU StudentDocuSign Envelope ID: 7AF0EFC4-96FC-40D7-B115-53B021D350E6

sections.heading: Page 6

sections.text:
A. The Student Body President, prior to the beginning of the Fall
Semester of any school year which has an election, shall call a
meeting with the Student Senate President and the SGA
Advisor in order to organize the opening of the Garnet & Gold
Voting Commission. During this meeting, the three shall decide
any Registered Student Organizations or Campus Entities that
shall have a designee on the Commission.
B. During the first week of the Fall semester that contains the
election, the Student Body President shall issue an executive
order that shall formalize the Opening of the Commission. This
executive order shall detail the list of organizations which shall
require a designee, as well as the timeline to submit them.
C. Upon the appointment of all designees, the Student Body
President shall make it public the composition of the committee.
1113.4 Operations
A. The Commission shall work with campus and community
partners to maximize the voter turnout of the FSU Student Body
during the relevant election. These partnerships may include,
but are not limited to, voter registration drives, voter education
events, social media campaigns, and any other efforts that
would increase civic engagement.
B. The Commission may make and publish recommendations to
the Student Government Association on how to best further
civic engagement on campus.
C. The Board of Directors shall meet no less than once every two
weeks between the appointment of all designees and the end of
the relevant election. These meetings shall be open to the
public and subject to all requirements of SGA meetings. The
Chair shall schedule these meetings, with consent of the Board
of Directors.
D. Following the end of the election, the Garnet & Gold Voting
Commission shall present a report of voter turnout and civic
engagement to the Student Senate.DocuSign Envelope ID: 7AF0EFC4-96FC-40D7-B115-53B021D350E6

Chapter 605 Oglesby Student Union Board
History: Amended by the 45th Senate Bill 142. Revised by the 47th Senate Bill 163.
Revised by the 48th Senate Bills 90 and 159. Revised by the 49th Senate Bill 14. Revised
by the 51st Senate Bill 30. Revised by the 54th Senate Bill 117. Revised by the 59th Senate
Bill 3. Revised by the 62nd Senate Bill 70. Revised by the 71st Bill 79, 88, 91. Revised by the
75th Senate Bill 7.
All rules and policies pertaining to the Oglesby Student Union
Board must be consistent with pertinent state law, university
policies and procedures, and the A&S Guidelines.
605.1 This act shall be called the "Oglesby Union Board Reform Act of 2006."
605.2 Establishment of the Union Board
The Union Board, hereinafter referred to as the Union Board, is
established to provide students, faculty, and staff with activities,
programs, and services to be offered through the Oglesby Student Union
Complex. The Union Board shall represent the University community to
ensure that the facilities, services, and amenities offered by the Oglesby
Student Union Complex meet the needs and interests of their
constituents.
605.3 Union Board Membership
A. The Union Board shall consist of seventeen (17) voting members
1. Twelve (12) voting members shall be students approved by
the Union Board Selection Commission according to
Chapter 605.4 and elected by the student body in the
Spring Student Government Elections.
2. The remaining five (5) voting members shall be appointed
by the University President or designee.
B. Ex-Officio Members
1. The Student Body President or a designee, the Student
Senate President or a designee, and the Director of the
Oglesby Student Union shall be ex-officio, non- voting
members of the Union Board. The Union Board may
appoint additional ex-officio, non-voting members to the
Board as deemed necessary.
C. Terms of OfficeDocuSign Envelope ID: D0B75284-E878-4B95-BFB2-CA2839594FAB

sections.heading: Page 3
sections.text:
1. The terms of office for the student members of the Union
Board shall be for one year or until their successors are
elected and confirmed except in the case of an appointment
to fill a vacancy, in which case the appointment shall be for
the remainder of the unexpired term.
2. The terms of office for voting members appointed
by the University President shall be established in
the Union Board bylaws.
3. Ex-officio, non-voting members, appointed by the Board,
may serve on the Union Board for as long as the Board
shall see fit.
D. Student members of the Union Board may be removed for
cause at any time in accordance with the provisions of Student
Body Statutes Chapter 405.3.
605.4 Candidacy for Union Board Membership
1. The Union Board shall publicly advertise openings for
student members of the Union Board for the spring
elections. This shall be done a minimum of ten (10)
business days preceding the spring elections.
2. The Union Board shall coordinate interest meetings for all
interested applicants to learn about the responsibilities of
the Union Board. All applicants must attend an interest
meeting in order to qualify for candidacy.
3. The Chair of the Union Board shall forward a list of those
who attended the interest meeting to the Supervisor of
Elections two (2) business days before the filing deadline.
4. All candidates who file with the Supervisor of Elections for
the Union Board, must attend an orientation meeting
pursuant to 704.2 (I).
605.5 Election of Student Union Board Members
A. The names of the forwarded candidates shall be placed on the
ballot pending an official declaration of candidacy. This provision
may be altered pending conditions pursuant to Chapter 605.4 D
(5).
605.6 Organization of the Union Board
A. The Union Board shall adopt bylaws and rules for its
organization, administration and procedures.DocuSign Envelope ID: D0B75284-E878-4B95-BFB2-CA2839594FAB

sections.heading: Page 4
sections.text:
B. Election of Union Board Leadership
1. The Union Board shall elect a Chair and a Vice Chair,
both being a student member of the Board.
2. The election for Chair and Vice Chair of the Union Board
shall be conducted at the beginning of each new session
after the Spring election and upon the departure of the
existing chair and vice chair.
3. The election method and guidelines shall be established
within the Union Board Policy Manual.
C. Duties of the Union Board Leadership
1. The Union Board Chair shall:
a. Call and preside over all meeting and general
business of the Union Board.
b. Act as the spokesperson for the Union Board policies and
interests.
c. Appoint all members of the Union Board committees.
d. Appoint all liaison positions to the Oglesby
Student Union complex’s departments and
subsidiaries.
e. Attend all Oglesby Student Union complex staff meetings.
f. The Chair may only vote on general Union
Board business in the case of a tie.
g. The Chair shall also perform any other duties
delegated by a majority vote of the Union Board,
which do not violate any standing Student
Government or Union Board policies and/or
Statutes.
2. The Vice Chair shall:
a. Perform the duties of the Chair in the Chair’s absence.
b. Perform other duties delegated by the Chair of
the Union Board and/or according to the Union
Board bylaws.
D. Committees of the Union Board
1. The Union Board may establish committees.
2. The Union Board Chair shall appoint all committee
members. Members of such committees may include ex-
officio, non-voting individuals who are not members of the
Union Board.DocuSign Envelope ID: D0B75284-E878-4B95-BFB2-CA2839594FAB

sections.heading: Page 5
sections.text:
E. The Chair and Vice Chair of the Union Board may be removed by
a two-thirds vote of the Board.
F. The Union Board shall meet not less than once each month.
Meetings of the Board shall be publicly advertised at least twenty
four hours (24) prior to each meeting. Meetings held without
quorum cannot feature votes.
605.7 The Powers and Duties of the Union Board
A. Determine policies, program services, activities, amenities, and
facilities to be offered by the Oglesby Student Union Board and
throughout the Oglesby Student Union Complex.
B. Participate in the budgetary process for all Union departments such as:
1. Review individual department and subsidiary budgets.
2. Assess the effectiveness of program services, activities,
and amenities and facilities.
3. Present a budget request and justification for all Union
departments and subsidiaries to the Student Senate
each fiscal year as well as any supplemental requests.
4. Upon allocation by the Senate of the A&S Fee request, the
Union Board shall authorize the A&S Fee funds, in addition
to self-generated revenues to the appropriate Union budget
and any amendments.
C. Allocate all space in the Oglesby Student Union complex in
accordance with Union Board and University Policy.
D. Serve in an advisory capacity to all departments and subsidiaries
within the Oglesby Student Union Complex.
Chapter 809 Replacement & Renovation Accounts
809.1 The Oglesby Student Union and Campus Recreation will set aside 25
percent (a quarter of one percent) of the cost of the facilities (based on
the Markell Chart as provided by the FSU Office of Environmental Health
and Safety) for a replacement and renovation (R&R) account to be
transferred no later than June 1 of each fiscal year. These funds will be
used for depreciation of their respective facilities and budgetary
emergencies as well as for repair and replacement of furniture and
equipment. There will be two categories of R&R:DocuSign Envelope ID: D0B75284-E878-4B95-BFB2-CA2839594FAB

sections.heading: Page 6
sections.text:
A. Physical Plant (anything with a useful life over five (5) years as
defined by the FSU University Controller's Office).
B. Furniture and Equipment Replacement (anything with a useful life
less than or equal to five (5) years as defined by the FSU
Controller's Office).
809.2 Any expenditure from the R&R account up to $10,000.00 must be
approved by the Facility Director and Facility Board with notification given
to the Senate President, Student Body President and the Vice President
for Student Affairs.
809.3 Any expenditures from the R&R account over $10,000.00 must be
approved by a majority of the group consisting of the Facility Director,
Facility Board, Senate President, Student Body President, and Vice
President for Student Affairs. The Facility Board shall have only one (1)
vote.
809.4 In an emergency, and the absence of other individuals mentioned in 809.2
and 809.3, the Directors of Campus Recreation, and Oglesby Student
Union may expend funds with the approval of the Vice President for
Student Affairs.
809.5 The required contribution for R&R will have first priority on the self-
generated funds for the Oglesby Student Union and Campus Recreation.DocuSign Envelope ID: D0B75284-E878-4B95-BFB2-CA2839594FAB

400.2 Office of the Senate President
The Office of the Senate President shall consist of the Senate President, Senate
President Pro-Tempore and the Officers of the Senate, hence referred to as
Senate Officers. The Student Senate President shall be responsible for the duties
of all vacant Senate Officers.
A. There shall be a President of the Student Senate who shall be elected by
majority vote of the Senate from its membership immediately following fall
inauguration. The Student Senate President shall be the chief legislative
officer of the Student Body and shall perform duties as provided by law
and Student Senate Rules of Procedure.
B. There shall be a Student Senate President Pro-Tempore who shall be
elected by a majority vote of the Senate from its membership immediately
following fall inauguration. The Senate President Pro Tempore shall assist
the President of the Senate and perform duties as provided by law and by
Senate Rules of Procedure.
C. The Student Senate President and President Pro-Tempore’s seats shall
not come up for election during their respective terms as President and
Pro-Tempore. Upon the resignation or removal of the Student Senate
President or Pro-Tempore, they shall immediately vacate their seat, if the
term to which they were elected or appointed has expired.
D. There shall be a Senate Parliamentarian, who shall be appointed by the
Student Senate President, subject to confirmation by the Student Senate,
from outside the membership of the Senate and who shall serve at Student
Senate President’s discretion. The Parliamentarian shall attend the
Student Senate meetings and upon request, give advice on parliamentary
procedure and any applicable law(s). This individual shall maintain order
under the direction of the Student Senate President or Presiding Officer.
The Parliamentarian shall endorse strictly the rules relating to the
privileges of the chamber.
E. There shall be a Senate Clerk, who shall be appointed by the Student
Senate President, subject by the confirmation of the Student Senate, from
outside the members of the Senate and who shall serve at the Student
Senate President’s discretion. The Senate Clerk shall attend the Student
Senate meetings and mainly be responsible for distributing legislation,
ballots, messages and other literature to Student Senators within the
Chamber. The Clerk shall also perform any other duties that the Student
Senate President or President Pro-Tempore shall determine to be
necessary for these purposes.
F. There shall be a Senate Historian, who shall be appointed by the Student
Senate President, subject to confirmation by the Student Senate, from
outside the members of the Senate and who shall serve at the StudentDocuSign Envelope ID: 53D5D26C-8E6D-445E-BBFB-ECBEE8928469

sections.heading: Page 3
sections.text:
Senate President’s discretion. The Historian shall be responsible for taking
Senate Chamber minutes. The Historian, along with the Senate Press
Secretary, shall have the responsibility of publishing a Senate newsletter
to document Senate legislative actions and updates. The Historian shall
also perform any other duties that the Student Senate President or
President Pro-Tempore shall determine to be necessary for these
purposes;
G. There shall be a Senate Press Secretary, who shall be appointed by the
Student Senate President, subject to confirmation by the Student Senate,
from outside the members of the Senate and who shall serve at the
Student Senate President’s discretion. The Press Secretary shall be
responsible for maintaining the Senate social media presence and
outreach and create a weekly calendar of Student Senate funded or
related events. The Press Secretary shall work with committee chairs to
help inform the student body on committee meeting information. The Press
Secretary, along with the Senate Historian, shall have the responsibility of
publishing a Senate newsletter to document Senate legislative actions and
updates. The Press Secretary shall also perform any other duties that the
Student Senate President or President Pro-Tempore shall determine to be
necessary for these purposes.
a. The Senate Press Secretary Shall attend a training session with
the SGA Webmaster to ensure that postings are within the Florida
State University communications guidelines. This shall ensure that
the social media properly represents the Student Senate.
H. There shall be a Senate Chief of Staff, who shall be appointed by the
Student Senate President, subject to confirmation by the Student Senate,
from outside the members of the Senate and who shall serve at the
Student Senate President’s discretion. The Chief of Staff shall be
responsible for managing the deadlines and responsibilities of the Senate
Parliamentarian, Clerk, Press Secretary, and Historian. The Chief of Staff
shall also be in discussions with the Senate President and President Pro-
Tempore regarding any ambitions they hope to accomplish during their
terms. The Chief of Staff shall also perform any other duties that the
Student Senate President or President Pro-Tempore shall determine to be
necessary for these purposes.
G. I. During the summer meetings of the Senate, the Student Senate President
may select a temporary replacement for any appointed officer, if that
individual is absent during the session.
H. J. Upon the receipt of applications for a vacant appointed position as defined
by statutes 400.2 C, 400.2 D, and 400.2 E in the Office of the Senate
President, a screening process shall be overseen by the Senate President
to determine the most qualified candidate. The process shall be defined by
the following:
1. All candidates must receive an interview.DocuSign Envelope ID: 53D5D26C-8E6D-445E-BBFB-ECBEE8928469

sections.heading: Page 4
sections.text:
2. The interview shall be conducted in a standardized and
professional form for all candidates.
3. The interview shall consist of a basic questionnaire outlining the
candidate’s experience, qualifications, and goals for the respective
position.
4. No officer position shall be filled until it has been advertised
properly in accordance with Chapter 404.2 A.
a. All positions shall be advertised for at least one week on the
SGA Website in accordance with Chapter 404.2 C.
5. After all candidates have been interviewed, the Senate President
may appoint and forward a candidate, who they deem most
qualified, to the floor of the Student Senate for confirmation.DocuSign Envelope ID: 53D5D26C-8E6D-445E-BBFB-ECBEE8928469

Chapter 814 The RSO Organizational Fund Act of 2023
History: Created by 75th Student Senate Bill 68.
814.1 There shall be an account known as the “Organizational Fund,” which shall be
administered by the Student Body Treasurer and be available for newly formed,
returning, or otherwise revitalized RSOs to apply for start-up funds as they are
established.
814.2 The Student Body Treasurer shall maintain an application on the SGA website
where RSOs may apply for organizational funds and shall determine whether an
RSO shall receive funding
A. The application shall open at the start of the new fiscal year and shall
remain open until all of its finds are depleted.
B. Upon receipt of an application for organizational funds, the Student Body
Treasurer must, within one (1) week, schedule a public hearing with
representatives from the RSO to determine the fiscal responsibility of the
request.
1. In the event that the Student Body Treasurer has a conflict of
interests with the applicant, pursuant to SBS 205.3, or is otherwise
unable to schedule a hearing, the Deputy Treasurer shall hear the
request. In the event that the Deputy Treasurer also has a conflict
of interest or is unavailable to schedule the hearing, the Student
Senate Finance committee shall hear the request.
C. At the organizational fund request hearing, applicants must present a
plan detailing how they intend to use the requested funding. The
Treasurer or Deputy Treasurer must create a comprehensive funding
recommendation for the Senate’s review. The funding recommendation
must include a line-item quote of the applicable organization’s request.
D. The Student Body Treasurer must report their recommendation of funds
to be allocated to the Chair of the Student Senate Finance Committee to
draft a consent resolution detailing the disbursement of funds in
alignment with the Student Body Treasurer’s recommendation. This
resolution shall be sent to the Student Senate Finance Committee placed
on the Consent Calendar within twenty-four (24) hours of the receipt of
said recommendation by the Finance Chair. Upon receiving a funding
recommendation from either the Student Body Treasurer or Deputy
Treasurer, the Chair of the Student Senate Finance Committee shall
immediately draft a consent resolution in alignment with the received
recommendation. This resolution shall be directly placed on the Consent
Calendar for the subsequent Senate meeting. The resolution must be on
the Consent Calendar no later than twenty-four (24) hours following the
receipt of the initial recommendation.DocuSign Envelope ID: A80963A7-B878-4D50-89DD-3EF7F7BFE4CA

sections.heading: Page 3
sections.text:
1. If the Deputy Treasurer hears the request, then they will forward
their recommendation to the Chair of the Student Senate Finance
Committee in accordance with this section. All information
provided in the recommendation shall be presented in the senate
meeting.
2. If the Student Senate Finance Committee hears the request, they
shall determine their recommendation and the Chair of the
Student Senate Finance Committee shall draft a consent
resolution to be placed on the Consent Calendar without first
being heard in the Finance Committee.
3. Amendments to this consent resolution shall require a two-thirds
(2/3) vote to pass.
814.3 Guidelines on Use of Organizational Funds
A. The Organizational Fund shall be intended to finance materials integral to
the success of a new, returning, or otherwise revitalized RSOs, including
but not limited to: flyers, tablecloths, printing, nametags, or any items
necessary for the RSOs mission.
B. A single RSO may receive up to $300 $500 from the Organizational Fund
each fiscal year.
C. RSOs that received A&S fees in the previous fiscal year shall not be
eligible to receive money from the Organizational Fund.
D. Organizations applying for the Organizational Fund should demonstrate a
financial need for start-up costs during the organizational fund request
hearing. A good faith effort shall be made to prioritize funding for
organizations that have not received A&S fees in the previous fiscal year.DocuSign Envelope ID: A80963A7-B878-4D50-89DD-3EF7F7BFE4CA
